articles.title: Jewish Dems in Michigan question place in party
articles.summary: Jewish Democrats in Michigan are facing a moment of reckoning in the Democratic Party as they grapple with a Senate nominee who has alienated some Jewish voters and with broader questions about their place in the party amid a rise in antisemitism. Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory over moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) earlier…
articles.body:
Jewish Democrats in Michigan are facing a moment of reckoning in the Democratic Party as they grapple with a Senate nominee who has alienated some Jewish voters and with broader questions about their place in the party amid a rise in antisemitism.

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory over moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) earlier this month has thrust those questions into the national spotlight , with some Jewish Democrats openly wrestling with whether to back their party’s nominee despite having reservations about his rhetoric on Israel and response to recent antisemitic incidents.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel (D), one of the state’s top Jewish elected officials, described some of those concerns in a recent interview with The Atlantic’s David Frum, saying many Michigan Jews feel increasingly unwelcome in their party and cast aside because of their belief that Israel has a right to exist.

“And so for a lot of us, you know, we feel really isolated. Like, do we have a home in the Democratic Party anymore?” Nessel said in the podcast released Wednesday.

Nessel was absent from the state party’s nominating convention on Saturday, announcing ahead of time that she would skip the gathering after a spring convention drew attendees who chased and shouted at Jewish and pro-Israel Democrats, sometimes preventing them from speaking.

She also said she feared the presence of five members of the state’s Democratic Party who had been criminally indicted for acts of vandalism, terrorism, harassment and intimidation against the Jewish Federation of Detroit and elected Jewish officials in their homes. The attorney general said the state party “seemingly are refusing to even suspend their membership to allow them to come to convention.”

“How are you supposed to feel, if you are an elected person, and who is a Democrat in Michigan, and you want to go to the convention, and you know those people are going to be there?” Nessel said on the podcast.

A spokesperson from the Michigan Democratic Party told The Hill on Sunday that “the party asked the individuals under criminal indictment not to attend the convention and they complied. ”

Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel touted the unity on display at the convention on Saturday and said the party is taking the concerns of Jewish Democrats seriously.

“As we saw at yesterday’s convention, Michigan Democrats are united heading into this election, and that includes a real, sustained commitment to earning the support of Jewish voters across our state,” Hertel said in a statement Sunday.

“We are committed to ensuring Democrats from every community feel safe and welcome within our party, including Jewish members, and that’s why we are taking seriously concerns Jewish Democrats have raised about antisemitism and safety, expanding regular dialogue with Jewish community leaders and the Jewish Caucus, and ensuring our candidates are showing up directly in Jewish communities across Michigan. We will continue these efforts through the election and beyond,” he continued.

Joan Lowenstein, endorsements chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, recalled that at the spring convention some of El-Sayed’s supporters became “not violent, but vociferously anti-Jewish and anti-Israel in supporting him,” which she said made many Jewish Democrats at the convention feel uncomfortable and like “they were being forced out.”

“In a way, it’s like being in any kind of club where you’ve been a longtime member and you’ve been loyal to the club, and all of a sudden, somebody comes in and tries to force you out,” Lowenstein told The Hill ahead of Saturday’s convention.

“I think there are many Jews, and I consider myself among them, who are going to stay in the club,” Lowenstein said. “There are others who say, ‘Look, this is a betrayal.’ People really feel betrayed … by seeing that a lot of our Democratic leaders are not standing up for us.”

The concerns are coming into sharper focus as Michigan Democrats wrestle with whether to back El-Sayed’s candidacy. Nessel told Frum she’s having conversations with Jewish Democrats who plan on backing the GOP candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), but for many Democrats — including Nessel — the choice is not so clear, since Michigan is seen as an essential seat for Democrats to win in November if they want to take control of the Senate.

“I will amputate my right arm before I fill in the oval next to Mike Rogers’s name,” Nessel said. “I think that keeping a Republican majority in the Senate is incredibly dangerous. I think Mike Rogers would be a rubber stamp for all of the worst excesses of the most corrupt administration we’ve ever had in American history. So he is a danger.”

But Nessel has not embraced El-Sayed’s candidacy either. El-Sayed has consistently condemned antisemitism, but he faced pushback for his response to the antisemitic attack earlier this year at Michigan’s largest synagogue, Temple Israel.

After initially condemning the attack, he released a subsequent video statement in which he tied the attack to Israeli military activity, noting the attacker had family in Lebanon who died in an airstrike and saying, “hurt people hurt people.”

Nessel said she and some other Democrats have concerns about that statement and the fact that until recently, El-Sayed stood by the remarks. El-Sayed on Saturday apologized for the comments.

“I made a mistake,” El-Sayed said during an appearance before the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus at the state party’s convention in Lansing. “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”

In a statement to The Hill, a campaign spokesperson said El-Sayed is having “good conversations” with Jewish leaders and will continue to do so.

“Abdul is grateful for a weekend of good conversations, and he’ll continue to be actively engaged with Jewish leaders across Michigan to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate, and put a much-needed check on Trump’s reckless agenda,” the spokesperson said Sunday.

The conversation resurfaced last week after Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has campaigned for El-Sayed, suggested violence could befall Jewish Americans if they continue to support Israel. As he was making the comments, a photo of Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss — the only Democrat in the state Legislature’s upper chamber and the nominee for Stevens’s current House seat — appeared on the screen in Israel surrounded by Israeli flags.

The incident was broadly condemned, including by El-Sayed , who has said he has no plans to campaign with Piker, but some criticized the nominee’s statement for not going far enough to distance himself from the streamer.

Michigan-based political consultant Adrian Hemond described Jewish Democrats as fitting into one of three buckets: “Group one is the ‘hell nos.’ Group two … [is] the want-to-get-to-yes category,” and group three includes “folks who have fallen in line.”

Hemond pointed to Moss as an example of the second group, an elected Democrat who, in his telling, “wants to get to yes” but has not been able to do so yet.

“A lot of people have really, really ambivalent feelings about this race,” Hemond said. “They think that Abdul’s an antisemite. They also think that the president sucks, and that it would be good to have a check on him in Washington. And so they’re sort of stuck between those two things.”

Josh Pasek, a professor of communication and media and political science at the University of Michigan, said Jewish Americans tend to be a very politically engaged group but may struggle to support a candidate if they disagree with them on social issues.

“That’s going to create a lot of structural ambivalence in voters. That’s a lot of what I think we’re seeing with this homelessness sense,” Pasek said.

Pasek said it’s hard to predict the political fallout, but he expects some Jewish voters will stay home while others will leave the Senate race blank.

Some Jewish Americans are single-issue voters on Israel, Pasek said, but those voters tend to fall on the political right, and most are “many-issue voters, so that is something that I think is going to have to be wrestled with over time.”

“Where the line is between what’s a policy dispute on Israel and where it gets to the point that somebody’s sufficiently anti-Israel that it is either problematic to one’s Judaism or feels antisemitic or something like that, is going to vary a lot across Jewish voters broadly, but Jewish voters in Michigan in particular, and that I think is going to be the inflection point that decides how impactful this all is,” Pasek said.

The conflict has been playing out on an institutional level as well. Lowenstein, as chair of endorsements for Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, described a fiercely divided caucus as its members question, for the first time since the group was founded in 2019, whether to back the Democratic general election candidate.

“Our caucus is not very old,” Lowenstein said. “So, in the past, I can’t think of any Democratic nominee that we have not endorsed.”

Lowenstein said she can’t say with certainty what the committee will decide, but Jewish voters have expressed concerns about rising threats of antisemitism, and she thinks the caucus will take those concerns seriously in making an ultimate decision.

“I do not know how it will actually come out because as I said, people are divided. I would say looking at it now, talking to members of our caucus, I don’t think that the people who support our caucus — the Democratic Jewish voters — I don’t think they want us to endorse El-Sayed.”

“Our caucus is never going to endorse a Republican. We are the Democratic Jewish caucus,” she added. “But, at the same time, there are so many people who feel so threatened by El-Sayed that there is just no way that — I think that we would lose our heart, the heart of what the caucus is all about, for us to go against the very strong feelings that so many in our caucus have.”

articles.title: Mark Walter scandal, LA Lakers sale raise concern about ownership in pro sports
articles.summary: Billionaire Mark Walter’s purchase of the Los Angeles Lakers and his subsequent forced sale of the team less than a year later amid allegations of financial crimes at his companies are sparking fresh concern about who owns the biggest brands in pro sports. It is also highlighting how clubs are being leveraged as profit-driving mechanisms…
articles.body:
Billionaire Mark Walter’s purchase of the Los Angeles Lakers and his subsequent forced sale of the team less than a year later amid allegations of financial crimes at his companies are sparking fresh concern about who owns the biggest brands in pro sports.

It is also highlighting how clubs are being leveraged as profit-driving mechanisms for some of the world’s richest people.

Walter, who made his billions in the insurance business and until this summer owned stakes in the Lakers, Los Angeles Dodgers and the English Premier League’s Chelsea, is reportedly under investigation by the federal government for alleged tax irregularities and failure to report billions in financing for key portions of his businesses.

His abrupt sale of the Lakers to an ownership group that includes Josh Kushner, the brother of President Trump’s son-in-law, is raising suspicion Walter is attempting to curry favor with the federal government and avoid the harshest of possible punishments.

Walter is hardly the first billionaire sports magnate to face scrutiny. His case, however, is underscoring what critics say is a growing danger in the accelerating corporatization of pro sports.

Insufficient guardrails vetting the financing of potential club buyers are a growing problem, critics say, and they are contributing to a widening disconnect between the sports ownership class and fans.

“There is probably no drier topic than billionaire debt service for everyday people, but we know for sure that fans are a more than a little bit tired of seeing their favorite teams treated like assets as opposed to community goods,” said Will Norton, director of the McCormack Center for Sport Research and Education at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. “These teams are becoming so expensive that you simply have to look to open up avenues to capital that otherwise would look like precarious choices for the long-term health of the club.”

More franchises than ever in the NFL, NBA, NHL and other leagues are partially owned and controlled by either private equity firms, owners who live and do business hundreds of miles away from a club’s home city or top executives with financial priorities that have little to do with the sports brands they own.

The result has been an ecosystem in which fan experience is suffering, and ownership groups are placing short-term return on investment over hometown pride and roster development.

Walter’s scandal is unique in that his businesses involve multiple franchises in several top sports leagues.

The Dodgers, perennial winners in the National League, have benefited in recent years from a major bargain on the team’s most recent media rights deal brokered by Walter.

The deal freed up millions for the franchise to spend aggressively on top talent and build arguably the most elite roster in baseball while ticket prices skyrocketed and wealthy celebrities packed Dodger Stadium’s most desirable seats.

The club’s financial strategy and others like it are at the center of a potential crisis facing MLB this offseason as its players union and owners stall out on a new collective bargaining agreement, a stalemate that most around the sport expect will end in a prolonged lockout.

Many attribute the arms race in baseball, and other pro sports, to the growing presence of private equity in the MLB, NBA, NFL and other leagues.

Top investment and venture capital firms now hold at least a partial stake in more than 70 clubs across North America alone, according to a recent study from the CFA Institute.

Internationally, governments are also spending aggressively on sports, most notably the Saudi Public Investment Fund, which has poured billions into niche sports such as golf and boxing and more popular global sports like soccer.

In the U.S., the presence of private equity is leading to more pressure than ever on ownership groups to raise larger sums of capital for better coaches, new stadiums and top talent.

Phoenix Suns owner Mat Ishbia is currently facing litigation from other minority owners in his club alleging he is using the team as a “personal piggy bank” to fund less profitable ventures in his portfolio.

Ishbia’s business partners also argue he cut them out of a deal granting naming rights for the team’s arena to his mortgage business.

“This all does start to raise questions about to what extent these leagues are properly vetting owners and potential owners,” said Mark Conrad, director of Fordham University’s sports business program. “Very few people can write a check for $12 billion. So, the idea of a hometown family owning a team is very passe, and the amount of money [required to buy a team] is a big part of it.”

Around the country, fans have grown increasingly frustrated with ownership groups in top leagues that have asked for billions in tax breaks for new stadiums, sold broadcasting rights for games to expensive paywalled streaming platforms and invested more in elite experiences for deep-pocketed fans.

Portland, Ore., faces a unique situation with the Trail Blazers ownership in the coming months.

The Blazers are owned by private mega-investor Tom Dundon, but the team’s home arena is the property of the city.

The two sides are currently negotiating how much the city should underwrite a planned renovation of the Moda Center, which is expected to come with a price tag of more than $300 million.

The standoff is leading many fans there to fear that if no deal is stuck by the end of the team’s current lease, one of the city’s only professional sports clubs could leave town.

It’s a problem that cities such as St. Louis, San Diego and Oakland have fallen victim to in recent years.

In those cases, observers say, smaller market teams are losing beloved franchises because they do not offer a big enough, or fast enough, return for wealthy ownership groups.

“Part of the problem is we still don’t have hard numbers behind the valuation of these teams to justify the amount that’s being paid [to keep them in a market]. We’ve got a different class of owners now, and the process hasn’t evolved with it,” said Cade Massey, an expert at the Wharton School’s operations, information and decisions department.

“The entities that are getting involved are widely more sophisticated now. And I’m sure all of the leagues, if they weren’t before, they’re thinking about this now,” he added.

College football kicked off this weekend, and the debate about player eligibility has never been more heated. Several major conferences such as the Big Ten and SEC are trying to ban players who were drafted by NFL teams last spring but were cut from pro rosters and still have NCAA eligibility from returning to college teams. The issue gets to the heart of NCAA’s lack of antitrust protection, opening it to litigation from players who wish to return to college or transfer to new schools. It also underscores the timeliness of the Protect College Sports Act, which senators are expected to vote on when they return from recess after Labor Day.

Good Good Golf, a golf media company that exploded in popularity with young people after the coronavirus pandemic, is under fire for an advertisement the brand published depicting violence against a woman. Club manufacturer Callaway cut ties with the organization over the ad, and the PGA Tour said last week Good Good would no longer be a sponsor of one of its fall events in Austin. The ad and the backlash it received have sparked widespread debate in the sports business community about “cancel culture” online and the game of golf’s inclusivity as it relates to women and underrepresented groups.

The Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention is slated for next week, Sept. 9 and 10. The event will have some big competition as it looks to capture the news cycle: the NFL. The league’s first regular season game kicks off Wednesday, Sept. 7, with a Super Bowl rematch between the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots, and the following night will pit the San Francisco 49ers against the Los Angeles Rams in an NFC West showdown set to be streamed on Netflix. Major news networks are expected to cover the GOP convention thoroughly during the day, but how many eyeballs the party can tear away from the NFL in primetime remains to be seen.

Rep. Herb Conaway (D-N.J.), a doctor of internal medicine who is up for reelection this year, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Certainly, it’s football. But lately I watch more golf than I used to. I’m into it, and my son is I would say an avid golfer, so he’s always got it on. I see it a lot.”

“Oh now this is a little controversial. … How do I answer this question? … I have been a Dallas Cowboys fan since I was 7 years old. I played quarterback in high school and played No. 12 because it was Roger Staubach’s number. And my offensive line behaved in the way the Cowboys did in the ’70s in terms of slapping their pads before getting down.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up?

“It had to be Staubach. He always found a way to win a game. I figured if he got the ball in his hands at the end of the game, he would always find a way to get the Cowboys in the end zone. Never say quit, never die.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“For years I liked to root against Pittsburgh because of Super Bowl XIII. It was one of the sad days of my young life when they lost, when Jackie Smith dropped that ball in the end zone.”

Sports and politics are both full of cliches; what’s one that resonates with you?

“I’d have to say my high school basketball coach said the best way to lose is to rest on the field of victory, so you have to keep driving through straight to the end.”

In the era of name, image and likeness rights, Sports Illustrated surveyed more than 40 college football insiders to find out “what teams are really spending on players this season.” Some of the top spenders: the University of Miami, Texas Tech University and the University of Oregon.

As Major League Baseball builds stronger ties to prediction markets and gambling platforms, The Athletic’s Zack Meisel spoke with a number of pro baseball players who told him about threats and harassment they regularly receive from bettors on social media.

The Wall Street Journal has a new profile out highlighting the work of Los Angeles Rams general manager Les Snead, who the outlet writes “found a way to build a perennial contender by rethinking the market as a value investor.”

articles.title: This tiny farming town you’ve never heard of is helping Microsoft sell America on data centers
articles.summary: Quincy, Washington, leveraged Microsoft data centers to fund a new high school, hospital and aquatic center, but long-term water concerns loom.
articles.body: In central Washington, a farming town of roughly 8,100 people has become an unlikely showcase for America’s data-center boom. Quincy, long known for potato fields, apple orchards and food-processing plants, has spent two decades attracting some of the world’s largest technology companies. Microsoft began building data centers there around 20 years ago, drawn by affordable land, the region’s cool climate and abundant hydropower from the Columbia River. Now the town is becoming central to Microsoft’s response to a backlash against the facilities powering cloud computing and artificial intelligence. The company this year cited Quincy as proof that data centers can bring tangible benefits to the communities that host them, as residents elsewhere raise alarms over electricity prices, water use and limited local job creation. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM The economic gains are visible in Quincy. KUOW reported that years of data-center tax revenue have helped support a state-of-the-art high school and hospital. The city recently opened a new aquatic center, complete with a six-lane lap pool, lazy river and waterslides, and is planning a separate indoor sports complex. Data centers are not an employment engine on their own. A single facility can operate with 50 employees or fewer, KUOW reported. But Quincy has enough facilities that the sector has become a meaningful employer in aggregate, while also supporting construction, service businesses and the city’s broader tax base. TRUMP HEADS TOWARD UNLIKELY CLASH WITH CLOSE ALLY OVER FUTURE OF MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR INDUSTRY Microsoft says its new national approach will ask local utilities to set rates high enough to cover data-center energy use and grid upgrades without raising prices for residents. The company also says future facilities will use closed-loop cooling systems that recycle water rather than drawing from local supplies. Quincy already has such a system. Microsoft and the city partnered on a $31 million water-reuse utility that treats and recirculates cooling water. The EPA says the project reduces the company’s reliance on potable groundwater and saves an estimated 138 million gallons of water a year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Still, Quincy is not without skeptics. Former Mayor Patty Martin, according to KUOW, has warned that the town must look beyond its immediate economic gains and consider its long-term water and electricity needs, pointing to population growth, electric vehicles and changing snowpack as added pressures on the region. Quincy’s boom shows what data centers can bring to a small town and the questions communities must answer before they arrive.

articles.title: Newly unclassified Pentagon images show suspected drug boats as official issues deadly warning
articles.summary: Exclusive Pentagon photos show suspected drug-smuggling boats under U.S. military surveillance as Operation Southern Spear reaches 67 strikes at sea.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE – Newly unclassified Pentagon images show suspected drug-smuggling boats at sea, including vessels loaded with apparent narcotics. The images come as the department warned traffickers that the U.S. will continue hunting down those who threaten Americans, nearly a year after the Trump administration began striking suspected drug-trafficking vessels. "Nearly one year after the first strike, the message to narco-terrorists remains unchanged: if you traffic deadly illicit narcotics and threaten the American people, we hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you," Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. The photos, dated Oct. 27, Oct. 29 and Dec. 4, 2025, show the boats speeding through open water under U.S. military surveillance. DEM SENATOR ACCUSES PENTAGON OF MURDER WITH BOAT STRIKES TARGETING DRUG TRAFFICKERS Wilson said Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced traffickers to adapt their methods and removed "dangerous narcoterrorists." US MILITARY CONDUCTS MORE DEADLY STRIKES AGAINST VESSELS OF ALLEGED 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' "Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced trafficker adaptations, removed dangerous narcoterrorists, and demonstrated that the United States will use every lawful tool available to defend our Homeland and protect our communities," Wilson said. The Pentagon told Fox News Digital the operation has carried out 67 strikes, including the first strike on Sept. 2, 2025. US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK One of the most recent strikes came Aug. 25, when U.S. Southern Command said four alleged drug smugglers were killed aboard a fast boat operating along known trafficking routes in the Caribbean. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking," SOUTHCOM wrote in a post on X, saying the operation was carried out by Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere under the direction of Gen. Francis L. Donovan. US MILITARY KILLS THREE 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN LATEST LETHAL STRIKE ON VESSEL IN THE EASTERN PACIFIC "Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere continues executing precise, lethal operations against the cartels," Donovan said in a statement quoted in the post. "We will hunt, disrupt, and defeat these narco-terrorist networks." "SOUTHCOM is resolved to neutralizing cartel terror and violence throughout the region and into the U.S. homeland," he added. US MILITARY CONDUCTS STRIKE ON ANOTHER VESSEL CARRYING ALLEGED NARCO-TRAFFICKERS, KILLING 2 Days before the Caribbean strike, the U.S. military said two people were killed in a strike on a vessel in the Eastern Pacific. That was the first reported strike in more than two months. A video posted to X showed what appeared to be a moving boat before a flash filled the screen. Since the first strike last September, the Trump administration has targeted suspected cartel vessels in the Atlantic and Pacific that it says were carrying narcotics. PRESIDENT TRUMP’S DRUG CONTROL STRATEGY SETS THE PATH TO END THE DRUG CRISIS FOR GOOD Trump has described the fight as an "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has argued the attacks are necessary to stop drugs from reaching American communities and fueling fatal overdoses. The administration is also pursuing agreements with allied nations that could extend its campaign onto land in multiple Latin American countries. War Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to conduct joint operations against criminal groups on their soil, though Guatemala denied an agreement had been reached. Ecuador began similar missions with the U.S. in March. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Reuters, The Associated Press and Fox News Digital's Eric Mack contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Jesus was a radical': Progressives invoke Christ to sell left-wing agenda on campaign trail
articles.summary: Angie Nixon, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico are weaving faith into their Senate campaigns, drawing comparisons to Jesus and echoing the Moral Majority.
articles.body: Progressives seeking a seat in the Senate are taking a decades-old page from their Republican counterparts, using faith as a political tool to build connections with voters. Three progressive Democratic candidates running for the Senate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state Rep. James Talarico, share a penchant for bucking the Democratic establishment in their meteoric rise this midterm cycle. They have also incorporated their religions and faiths into their campaigns and messaging to voters, showing shades of the "Moral Majority" coalition that formed during the late 1970s in the GOP when former President Ronald Reagan was running as Republicans sought to tie policy to Christianity. PROGRESSIVE FLORIDA LAWMAKER ANGIE NIXON TOPPLES TRUMP IMPEACHMENT WITNESS IN DEM SENATE PRIMARY UPSET Nixon, who scored a major upset against Alexander Vindman, a major figure during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial who was backed by the Democratic establishment in Washington, D.C., has become a prime target for the GOP because of her connection to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). During a sermon last week at the Saint Paul AME Church of Jacksonville, Fla., Nixon, who will face Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., in November, contended that her "radical" positions were akin to those of Jesus Christ. "They are trying, y'all. They are trying … to label me as this extremist, this radical. But, you know, Jesus was a radical," Nixon said. EL-SAYED MAKES JESUS COMPARISON WHEN PRESSED ON SOCIALIST VIEWS: 'RADICAL IN HIS TIME, TOO' "And Jesus fought for — I mean, he pushed for the same things that I'm fighting for today, right? Right now, we're literally in a civil rights moment," she continued. "Whether or not people wanna believe it or not, but we are." She joined the DSA in June, prompting immediate backlash from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, which tied her to socialism, despite her denial that she’s a Democratic socialist. Nixon isn’t the only one of the three to make the same comparison. El-Sayed, during an appearance on the Progressive Christians Podcast that aired in May, similarly invoked Christ when asked about his policy positions. El-Sayed, who is Muslim and running in Michigan’s toss-up race against former Rep. Mike Rogers, was asked about the similarities between his faith and Christianity and why they were being targeted as radical. "Well, you know, Jesus, peace and blessings be upon him, was considered radical in his time, too," El-Sayed said. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY' "And there is a radical nature to being willing to stand forthright in a time of corruption, and I think it's important for all of us to realize that popularity and zeitgeist don't make truth. And we live in a time where people are trying to normalize corruption," he continued. Of the three, Talarico, who is running in the toss-up race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, has displayed his faith the most. He has been taking seminary classes to become a Presbyterian minister, and has blended Christianity with his policy platform since launching his candidacy last year. And like the others, Republicans have pounced on his use of faith as a point of attack, particularly in his defense of transgender children. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In pushing back against the Texas GOP’s newly signed anti-trans bill in 2021, Talarico argued Texas Republicans were trying to justify the measure "in the name of God's law." "The first two lines of the Bible, the first two lines in Genesis, use two different Hebrew words to describe God. One is the masculine Hebrew noun for divinity," Talarico said. "The second is the feminine Hebrew noun for spirit. God is both masculine and feminine, and everything in between." "God is non-binary," he said.

articles.title: Biden’s praetorian guard in the media now feigns concern about presidential fitness
articles.summary: I told you this was coming. I was right.
articles.body:
I told you this was coming . Many of those who promised during 2023 and early 2024 that Joe Biden was “sharp as a tack” are now deeply concerned about President Trump’s mental acuity. Those “We missed the story” mea culpas from a while back were never about contrition, or even real embarrassment. These people had no problem lying about Biden’s fitness — they just couldn’t get away with it any longer.

So they changed strategy. They started laying the groundwork to pretend later they had “learned their lesson” so they could go hard after the current president, despite having far less evidence.

MS NOW’s Jonathan Capehart, for example, remarked recently that “We should be talking about [Trump’s] mental acuity.”

“Why are we not talking about his mental acuity when we, when we … more people should be talking about it in the way they were giving President Biden hell for walking with a stiff gait,” he said.

A “stiff gait?” Biden was so badly out of it that federal prosecutors felt sorry for him and decided not to pursue him for crimes he admitted to on tape on the grounds that he was an “ elderly man with a poor memory .” As anyone who had eyeballs during that era can tell you, the problems went well beyond his awkward ambling. They were less “stiff gait” and more “ he’s talking to dead people again .”

The problems were real, and they were obvious — despite efforts by people like Capehart, who hosted Biden for extra-chummy softball questions about his fitness for office, to fool you into thinking otherwise.

“Why I get so enraged by this is, why is [Trump] being given a pass?” Capehart demanded. “He’s President of the United States! No other president would be able to survive.” It is a hollow commentary that downplays Biden’s evident senility while pushing hard to oversell Trump’s mostly longstanding peculiarities. And he does this after participating in a concerted effort to portray Biden as vibrant, cogent, and vigorous — all lies, of course. The simpler explanation is that Capehart cares about neither president’s health, nor does he care particularly for the truth.

Speaking of party collaborators, let us not forget Joe Scarborough, also of MS NOW, who remarked recently , “For a president who has always been erratic, as he turns 80, we are seeing some diminished capacities [as] with anybody who would turn 80.”

He added, “But that erraticism, we are seeing it exaggerated.”

For context, Scarborough was among those fighting to the last man in the last-ditch effort to save Biden’s reelection campaign. In 2024, as Biden lurched toward an uncontested renomination, Scarborough famously declared of Biden : “[H]e’s far beyond cogent. In fact, I think he’s better than he’s ever been, intellectually, analytically, because he’s been around for 50 years. … Start your tape right now because I’m about to tell you the truth. And f— you if you can’t handle the truth. This version of Biden, intellectually, analytically, is the best Biden ever. Not a close second.”

Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential race four months later after a debate revealed otherwise.

To be fair, Scarborough is not overselling Trump’s supposed dotage the way Capehart has been doing. He recently remarked that any suggestion that Trump “has dementia or is losing his mind or whatever” is ridiculous — which is true.

Then we have the Substack cohort of former newsmen, including John Harwood and Jim Acosta, both of whom have suggested recently that Trump’s body and brain are both spiraling.

“There’s no question … about his cognitive decline and whether he’s just a man in decline,” declared Acosta, who used to work for CNN. “I think that’s undoubtedly the case. I mean, if we’re not going to believe our own eyes and ears anymore.”

He added, “This is the stuff that they’re waving in everybody’s face about Joe Biden, and Joe Biden was not falling asleep all the time in front of the cameras the way Donald Trump is. I mean, it’s kind of embarrassing.”

Sorry, but Biden did most certainly fall asleep all the time .

Harwood, who used to work for CNBC, added “You’ve got the bruised hands, you’ve got the neck and got the face, one side of the face is sagging.”

“It’s a very dangerous moment,” said Acosta, “that I think we’re in the middle of right now.”

In 2024, at CNN, Acosta promoted the White House’s false claims that all the photos and videos of Biden’s decline were so-called “cheap fakes,” the work of dirty, nameless political operatives working through “right-wing media.”

“We’re hearing about, so-called cheap fakes,” Acosta said . “It’s playing out on right-wing media, Fox, New York Post, and so on. And all of this is to try to make the case that Biden is slipping. He’s confused and so on.”

As for Harwood, he was but one of many newsmen who threw a conniption fit after Special Counsel Robert Hur politely noted that Biden’s brains had turned into mashed potatoes. He was also impervious to evidence after an especially poor, rambling Biden press conference that had been called in February 2024, specifically to dispel concerns about the president’s mental fitness. Harwood declared : “Biden’s press conference showed the same thing his performance in office has shown for three years: He can do the job.”

Even after Biden’s disastrous performance in the June 2024 presidential debate, Harwood was one of the last to keep the faith, writing , “I do not consider Biden cognitively unfit for the presidency. He has been doing the job effectively for more than three years.”

Now is as good a time as any to remind you that even Jill Biden thought her husband was having a stroke during the debate . What is Harwood’s explanation for this?

Questions about Trump’s age and mental fitness are certainly fair game. But not from these people. They are liars who showed during the Biden administration that they have no integrity. They demanded that you doubt the evidence of your own eyes and ears. You are better off doing what you did back then, tuning them out and trusting your own judgment.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Vulnerable Dem's own audit admits Medicaid oversight failure amid massive statewide fraud scandal
articles.summary: Matt Dunlap's office acknowledged a significant deficiency in tracking MaineCare payments as JD Vance calls Maine a fraud capital of America.
articles.body: Maine's Democratic state auditor, Matt Dunlap, who is now pursuing a bid to represent Maine's 2nd Congressional District, released a report earlier this year sounding the alarm that the state's internal watchdog for its MaineCare program had a serious gap in utilization control. "[The Program Integrity Unit] could not provide documentation of the methodology used to identify projects and post-payment reviews performed in relation to surveillance of all Medicaid services provided under the State plan," the report reads, referring to the "PIU," the program's watchdog. The report’s release, which comes after revelations of healthcare fraud in Maine from federal investigators and a local whistleblower, puts renewed focus on Dunlap’s tenure as auditor and raises questions about Maine's past systems to detect fraud amid one of the country's most competitive congressional races. VANCE TURNS UP HEAT ON STATES WITH FEDERAL CASH THREAT OVER MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN In order to ensure that state programs are complying with federal requirements, the PIU, the watchdog, selects a set number of cases for review, picking those cases based on "data analytics." The report didn't expand on those analytics — but noted a key weakness. In addition to being unable to provide documentation of why those cases had been chosen for review, the process also didn't take into account possible misuse — by patients or by the companies that bill MaineCare. In the report's words, the PIU, the watchdog group, "does not document consideration of misutilization practices of beneficiaries or providers ... [and] may not provide adequate monitoring of all Medicaid services, resulting in potential noncompliance with Federal regulations." Dunlap's 2026 report also acknowledged that this particular reporting issue hadn't been caught before, noting that it had a "prior year findings: none" designation. When asked about the weakness and whether this was really the first time it had surfaced in an audit, Dunlap's campaign stressed that the report only narrowly applied to that particular weakness and that Dunlap had received praise — even from local Republicans — on his work identifying other liabilities. "As Auditor, Matt Dunlap has flagged many issues that date back to the LePage administration. He has been praised by local press and Republican leaders alike for his work to recommend ways to safeguard taxpayer dollars. Paul LePage should answer why his team didn't implement the recommendations of his own Auditors from when he was governor," Harry Burke, a spokesperson for the Dunlap campaign said in a comment to Fox News Digital, referring to the Republican nominee in the race, a former governor of Maine who served from 2011 to 2019. The campaign also observed that Dunlap himself, as an auditor, has little power to implement changes he flags as problematic. Decisions to remedy issues within Maine's programs lie within the departments themselves, although auditors can recommend specific changes. "The auditor's job is to be a fire alarm: identify the problems so that state agencies can act. For example, last year, his recommendations led to the arrest and prosecution of a procurement fraudster saving taxpayer dollars," Burke added. Despite his campaign's pushback, Dunlap has received backlash from Republicans for failing to stop fraud schemes that have caught national attention. TRUMP TASK FORCE IS TACKLING $250 BILLION IN GOVERNMENT FRAUD. IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED Dunlap first came into the role in 2021 despite lacking the credentials to become an auditor. After being installed, he had to resign after twice failing the needed tests to become a certified auditor. Even so, Dunlap returned to the role in November 2022 after passing the requisite exams. That track record has become a focal point for Republicans in the congressional race after the U.S. Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General revealed in January that the state had paid out at least $45.6 million in improper Medicaid payments for autism services. The findings only furthered concerns raised by a whistleblower in December. Christopher Bernardini, a former employee of Gateway Community Services, said his company had been defrauding Maine’s Medicaid program. According to Bernardini, the health services contractor had routinely filed false records about client visits, billing the state for services that Gateway had never provided. The compounding stories of fraud have captured the attention of figures like Vice President JD Vance, who highlighted them in a visit to the state on Monday. "How did Maine become one of the main capitals of defrauding the American taxpayer?’" Vance asked at a campaign event. "One of the answers is somehow you guys hired an auditor who is not actually an auditor and failed the auditor exam. Well, call it old-fashioned common sense, but if you want somebody managing your money, maybe they ought to actually meet the constitutional requirements to do the job," Vance said. Vance argued Dunlap’s track record should be disqualifying. "And for Matt Dunlap, if you’ve got a guy who cannot protect your tax dollars from fraudsters, who has turned your state into one of the fraud capitals of the United States of America, maybe you should be saying to Matt Dunlap, ‘You’re fired, not promoted to the United States Congress,’" Vance said. Previous years of reporting before Dunlap’s time as auditor also cast doubt on the office’s aggressiveness in uncovering fraud, hinting that the office’s zeal has declined under his watch. Notably, in the six years before Dunlap took over the reins in 2022, the state had identified that it had almost too many active fraud investigations. "Cases opened because of potential fraud, abuse, or questionable practices need improved supervisory review," several reports state. Audits going back to 2016 noted that the office had routinely taken on more cases than its resources and its staffing would allow for, leading to a lack of monitoring of individual cases. DR. articles.title: Pentagon erupts over classified leak of Iran war dissent
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ U.S. strikes Iran after monthlong pause ▪ Trump touts Venezuela oil deal ▪ House back in session ▪ GOP midterm convention frustrations The Pentagon is seething over a Washington Post report that top military leaders recently warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against extending large-scale Iran war operations. People familiar with a classified assessment prepared…
articles.body:
▪ U.S. strikes Iran after monthlong pause

The Pentagon is seething over a Washington Post report that top military leaders recently warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against extending large-scale Iran war operations.

People familiar with a classified assessment prepared for Hegseth told the Post that several combatant commanders have advised the Defense chief that prolonging operations against Iran is unsustainable and risks weakening the U.S.’s ability to address threats elsewhere, including on U.S. soil.

The warnings appear in the Aug. 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), detailed by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and the four-star commanders overseeing U.S. operations throughout Europe, Asia and Latin America, the Post reported Sunday.

Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell lambasted the report in a post on the social platform X .

“Publishing highly classified assessments from the Secretary’s orders book is a crime. It’s a betrayal of the force,” he said. “And much of what they’re publishing is inaccurate.”

Parnell said the Pentagon wants “candid” advice and disagreements are common.

“The Secretary sees them constantly. That’s how you run a real military. We are in great shape around the world. This story isn’t about readiness,” he said, alleging it is about “TDS,” an acronym that President Trump and his allies often use to mean “Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Washington Post military affairs reporter Dan Lamothe defended his colleagues’ work with a response to Parnell.

“Fact check: Independent journalism is not a crime,” he said. “It’s also especially important at a time when government officials are withholding key details and concerns about a war being fought on behalf of the American people with their taxpayer dollars.”

The Aug. 14 SDOB directs some U.S. forces currently deployed in the Middle East to remain through September and others into 2027, those familiar with the document told the Post.

The heads of U.S. European, Pacific and Southern Commands, along with the Navy’s top admiral, responded with a “non-concur” — signaling their disagreement with Hegseth’s order to extend their forces, the Post reported.

The report comes as the U.S. and Iran traded fire for the first time in almost a month. The war, now in its sixth month, has drained the Navy’s budget and significantly depleted U.S. stockpiles of missile interceptors and long-range precision missiles.

Throughout the conflict, U.S. ships, personnel, aircraft and equipment have been redirected from various parts of the world to the Middle East. The sources told the Post that this has limited the military’s ability to conduct missions and ensure proper training.

In addition to Parnell, other accounts on X with links to the Pentagon weighed in to slam the Post for reporting on classified information.

The account DataRepublican, which is run by Utah software engineer Jennica Pounds , a special government employee at the Defense Department, responded to Lamothe.

“This is one of the most serious leaks I have ever seen, and you are using this to score partisan points against Hegseth,” the account posted .

“The one without ethics here is the entire staff of the Washington Post who did not immediately turn in this traitor as soon as they received the material,” Pounds continued.

Adam D’Ortona , an active-duty Army lieutenant colonel who runs the account InfantryDort, accused the Post of working for the “enemies of the United States.”

“Worse, this isn’t gossip. Revealing where senior commanders believe forces are stretched, where they perceive risk, and which commitments they consider unsustainable gives an adversary information it can immediately exploit,” he wrote.

USA Today reported last year that D’Ortona works in Hegseth’s office.

In recent weeks, Trump has shifted from military threats to economic pressure against Iran, as the U.S. Navy has slowly expanded its control over the Strait of Hormuz, facilitating steady oil tanker traffic and keeping gas prices stable, though still high.

Centcom said last week that the U.S. had cleared the strait of all sea mines along internationally recognized transit routes.

U.S. forces late Sunday struck Iranian rocket launchers in waterway. U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins , a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command (Centcom), said two launchers were hit on Lark Island after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were seen preparing to launch rockets with sea mines in the strait.

Iran retaliated for the attack by launching missiles toward U.S. military sites in Jordan. The United Arab Emirates said it also intercepted an Iranian drone over its territorial waters.

A major flash flood has forced dozens of people to evacuate from the Grand Canyon , with water sweeping over large boulders, metal structures and debris. At least one person has died, and officials said about 15 people “may be missing or unaccounted for.”

Approximately 85 Americans are still missing following flash flooding on the border between Nepal and Tibet , a State Department spokesperson said Sunday. More than 900 people have been confirmed dead in the flooding. The spokesperson said the department isn’t aware of any confirmed U.S. citizen deaths so far.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is denying a report from The New York Times that migrants in immigration detention facilities have faced abusive or violent treatment or been denied medical care while in detention. DHS accused the Times of “fueling” an increase in assaults against immigration officers.

A pedestrian walks past a mural featuring oil wells in Caracas, Venezuela, on Aug 29, 2026. President Trump announced a deal giving the United States a stake in Venezuela’s oil reserves the day before.

FILL IT UP : Trump said he will “fill up” the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) following his deal for the U.S. to assume control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil.

“The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States,” he said in a post on Truth Social on Sunday.

The president announced on Friday that he reached the deal with the Venezuelan government , which has been led for months by interim President Delcy Rodríguez since the U.S. operation to capture former leader Nicolás Maduro .

The planned U.S. stake represents about 21 percent of Venezuela’s total proven oil reserves, which are the largest in the world. Trump said he the deal comes at “no cost” to U.S. taxpayers.

A U.S. official told The Hill that Rodríguez granted a private company 100-year “concessions” for oil fields containing 63 billion barrels of proven reserves. The company is reportedly a joint venture between the U.S. government and Alejandro Betancourt López , whose heads Venezuela’s second largest private oil producer, North American Blue Energy Partners.

The official said the U.S. government will get 55 percent of the “effective output” from the joint venture.

Rodríguez shared more details of the deal in a late-night speech to her nation on Saturday, heralding the deal as “historic” and key to reviving Venezuela’s economy and increasing government revenue. She said it will lead to the development of 17 strategic oil fields and more than $200 billion in tax revenue.

Allies of Trump praised him for the agreement, while Democrats expressed skepticism that it would cause consumers to see a reprieve from the high gas prices that have been in place for months.

“Will prices come down for Americans? Who knows but likely not as much as Trump has forced them up thru his idiotic Iran War,” said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.).

LOOK WHO’S BACK : The House is returning to Washington this week after a monthlong recess, as lawmakers are hoping to pass legislation averting a government shutdown.

The top item on the House’s agenda is the Senate-passed continuing resolution to keep the government open beyond the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30. If passed, the bill would fully fund government departments and agencies through Dec. 11, after the midterms.

House Republican leaders are hoping to bring the bill to the floor under a fast-track process known as a suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority. The legislation is expected to have wide support from Republicans and Democrats, as it did in the Senate.

The House previously passed its own stopgap funding measure that would keep the government open through Dec. 4.

‘REBUKE OR PUNISHMENT’ : Trump said on Sunday that “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker will be reported to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for saying that Trump-endorsed candidates have had “mixed results” in GOP primaries this year.

Welker reportedly discussed Trump’s endorsement record during a preshow live shot on NBC’s Washington, D.C., affiliate. Trump pushed back in a post on Truth Social, noting the successes last week of Sen. Darline Graham (R) in South Carolina’s GOP Senate runoff and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R) in Oklahoma’s GOP gubernatorial runoff.

“How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump said.

Trump has sparred with Welker before, ending an interview with her early in June as she pressed him on his unfounded claim of the California gubernatorial primary being “rigged.”

The president’s endorsed candidates have overwhelmingly won their primaries, though he has taken several high-profile losses this year, including in five GOP gubernatorial primaries.

President Trump gives a thumbs up after arriving on Air Force One on Aug. 28, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md.

‘TRUMP-A-PALOOZA’ : Details are finally starting to come out about the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention that it plans to hold next week, and some party members are expressing frustration with the logistics.

The Hill’s Julia Mueller and Helen Huiskes report some Republicans are quietly upset that the event came together so quickly and that lawmakers are reportedly expected to contribute $25,000 to attend.

A GOP operative told The Hill that while Trump has been talking about the convention for a year, lawmakers and candidates haven’t had long to plan for it.

“Lot of things made this very hasty that didn’t need to happen,” the operative said.

The convention is set to take place in Dallas on Sept. 9 and 10. The Republican Party hasn’t held a midterm convention before. The Democratic Party did hold midterm conventions a few times in the 1970s and 1980s and considered holding one this year but ultimately decided against it.

While Trump and the GOP are hoping that the convention can be a rallying point for the party ahead of the midterms, Mueller and Huiskes note a few other points of concern for the party.

The convention is scheduled to take place simultaneously with the first two NFL games of the season and runs up against the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, raising questions about whether it will ultimately get enough attention to be worthwhile. The event also risks pulling candidates away from the campaign trail during a key stretch.

Dallas’s city agencies, meanwhile, are working quickly to ensure security is running effectively for the convention.

Sima covers her face at the grave of her six-month-old granddaughter who died during the winter, in Kabul, Afghanistan, on Aug. 12, 2026.

A GRAVE PICTURE : Afghans both inside and outside the United States are facing a difficult reality five years after Afghanistan fell to the Taliban as U.S. forces withdrew from the country.

The Trump administration has drastically reined in the pathways for Afghans to arrive in the U.S. over the past year and a half. In one of its first moves, the White House suspended refugee processing except for white South Africans.

DHS has moved to strip temporary protected status for Afghans, which ended protections for more than 8,000 people.

The administration also began the process of reviewing and revoking some special immigrant visas (SIVs) for Afghans who worked alongside the U.S. military and government as interpreters, special operations partners and local embassy staff.

The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports that things have gone from bad to worse for Afghans and their advocates.

As the U.S. evacuated in August 2021, the Taliban quickly returned to power and now controls the country. Afghan women, who were previously able to attend school and pursue careers, are now shut off from most parts of public life.

Afghans who have made it to the U.S. live in a precarious state, Beitsch notes. Those who have received an SIV or green card have received letters warning them that the basis for that status has been revoked .

“Five years ago, this was a crisis. Everything was on fire, nobody had a plan, and the failures were failures of capacity. That is not what this is anymore,” Shawn VanDiver , the president and founder of #AfghanEvac, told reporters.

“It is a deliberate choice, grounded in policy this government has not had the courage to verbalize or brief,” he said.

A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with the space observatory Roman Telescope lifts off from launch complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla., on Aug. 30, 2026.

And finally … NASA has launched a new space telescope considerably more powerful than the famed Hubble that’s been in orbit around the Earth since 1990.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is designed to survey the universe a thousand times faster than Hubble, according to NASA . It will also capture panoramic images with a field of view about 100 times larger, Accuweather reports .

The telescope is named for Nancy Grace Roman , the first female chief of astronomy at NASA who is known as the “mother” of Hubble for her key role in planning for it. It will remain in orbit for at least five years, with a possible five-year extension.

NASA expects to release the telescope’s first images by early next year.

articles.title: Why the left can’t stop obsessing over Trump
articles.summary: Trump’s supporters aren’t the mystery — his critics are more interesting.
articles.body:
Millions of Americans insist they are exhausted by President Trump. Yet many know exactly what he posted yesterday, what he said that morning, and what cable news is arguing about tonight.

They complain the media covers him too much, yet they continue clicking, watching, reposting and debating him. If Americans are so tired of Trump, why not stop paying so much attention to him?

Trump’s supporters aren’t the mystery. They voted for him. They want to hear what he has to say.

His critics are far more interesting. Many people who wish Trump would disappear from public life nevertheless follow him relentlessly. They monitor his speeches, dissect his social media posts and debate his every move. Politics alone doesn’t explain that contradiction. Psychology helps explain the rest.

Behavioral psychologists have long known that unpredictable rewards are among the strongest forces governing human attention. Casinos rely on the same principle, known as intermittent reinforcement. When people don’t know what comes next, they keep checking. Politics isn’t gambling, but attention to it often follows the same pattern.

For nearly a decade, Trump has supplied something modern politics rarely offers: genuine uncertainty about what comes next. Tomorrow may bring a policy announcement, a personnel decision, a courtroom development, an impromptu exchange with reporters or the renaming of some major body of water .

Whatever it is, supporters and critics alike expect something worth their attention. That uncertainty keeps both sides engaged. Supporters watch because they hope something important has happened. Critics watch because they worry it has. Different emotions produce the same behavior, and both sides remain fixed on the same person.

Few public figures generate ratings, clicks, and debate as reliably as Trump. The media don’t simply report on Trump — they often amplify him. News organizations compete for audience attention. Even outlets that say they want to move on frequently find themselves pulled back because audiences continue watching. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle. Trump says or does something unexpected. News organizations rush to cover it. Critics condemn it. Supporters defend it. Television panels debate whether the story deserved so much attention, only to give it even more. Before long, the conversation about Trump becomes larger than the event that started it.

Attention is not the same as approval. People naturally devote more attention to uncertain situations than predictable ones, and politics is no exception. As long as Americans believe tomorrow may bring a consequential Trump development, millions will continue checking today’s headlines, whether they support him or oppose him. This also helps explain why predictions of “Trump fatigue” rarely come true. People who say they want less Trump often become the ones most determined not to miss the next development. They remain locked in the cycle they claim to dislike.

Of course, Trump commands attention because he is president. But that doesn’t fully explain what we’ve witnessed over the past decade. Every president dominates headlines. Few have generated this level of sustained public anticipation. Trump has an unusual ability to make supporters and critics alike believe that the next headline could matter.

That matters because attention is political currency. Before politicians persuade voters, they first have to capture attention. Every hour spent arguing about Trump’s latest statement is an hour not spent discussing someone else’s agenda. Whether people support him or oppose him, they continue making him the focal point of American politics.

For years, Trump’s critics have argued that the country needs to move on from him. Yet many continue giving him exactly what every politician seeks: attention.

Ironically, some of the people most determined to diminish Trump’s influence may be helping preserve it. Trump’s greatest political skill may not be persuasion, ideology, or even charisma. It is his remarkable ability to command attention.

In politics, winning attention often comes before winning arguments. Until people understand why they keep giving Trump so much of it, they will continue sustaining the very phenomenon they say they want to escape.

Jonathan Alpert is a psychotherapist and author of Therapy Nation .

articles.title: How Meta got away with a $17.1 billion slap on the wrist
articles.summary: The lesson: don’t settle. Make Meta face a jury.
articles.body:
On Aug. 26, just eight days into one of the biggest trials in social media history, Meta agreed to settle with 47 states, D.C. and U.S. territories. The social media giant agreed to pay $12.19 billion over 10 years , which could rise to $17.1 billion if TikTok and YouTube agree to comparable terms. (A $1 billion settlement with Texas was reached the same day.)

The settlement marks the largest state consumer protection settlement in history, outside of Big Tobacco.

The coalition of states originally sought approximately $200 billion . Meta’s lawyers said they were exposed to as much as $1.4 trillion in damages. This case was poised to reshape not just Meta but social media as we know it. Instead, Meta agreed to pay less than a tenth of what the states had asked for.

As one of the early architects of social networking , I’ve been building social media platforms since the 1990s. For nearly 30 years I’ve been doing it without targeted ads or algorithmic manipulation. The industry veered astray when an “engagement at all costs” attitude and surveillance advertising took the reins. This settlement was a chance to take the reins back. It goes partway, but it stops short.

Meta already lost two landmark cases this year. In March, a jury in Los Angeles found Meta and YouTube liable in the first personal injury trial over addictive design. A similar case against Meta in New Mexico led to nearly $1 billion in penalties .

In this latest and biggest trial, the opening statements presented the case regarding intentional harmful design. “Hook the users. Hold them for as long as they can. Harvest their data. Hide the truth from the public when making public statements,” California Deputy Attorney General Megan O’Neill stated during the trial . “Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids.”

The star witness was Arturo Bejar , a former Meta safety engineer and whistleblower. He testified that Meta employed a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy for its underage users. He told the jury that “Instagram changed from a product that you use to a product that uses you.” The states’ attorneys revealed an email from 2021 that Bejar sent to Mark Zuckerberg, which showed that more than half of teens surveyed had a harmful experience on Instagram in the prior week. Zuckerberg never replied.

The company settled before Zuckerberg was slated to take the stand. That alone says how strong the case was.

The comparison between tobacco and social media was made several times. In 1998, the four biggest cigarette makers settled cases brought by 46 states for $206 billion. The real transformation was the end of cigarette marketing to kids. Thirty-six percent of high school kids smoked in 1997. Today, it’s 1.4 percent . But it never changed the addictive nature of the cigarette itself.

This settlement is supposed to go further and change the product. It requires several changes for users under 18, including: a maximum limit of two hours per day; no access between midnight and 6:00 a.m.; no push notifications during school hours or overnight; no public “like” counts; and no beauty filters. A parent can switch the time limit and overnight block off , and direct messages are exempt from all of it .

These are two major functional misses. One, algorithmically manipulated newsfeeds remain in place for users under 18, with only an opt-out choice (opt-outs are rarely selected). This is the core of Meta’s business model: It predicts the content that keeps kids scrolling and serves them more of it. Keeping this engine intact is a massive and unacceptable gap. Two, “robust” age assurances are required to remove any users under age 13. However, the method is left entirely to Meta .

Meta will celebrate this as a victory. Revenue at the company last year was approximately $200 billion . A $17 billion settlement paid over 10 years is less than 1 percent of that each year. Spread across 47 states, D.C. and the territories over 10 years , the payments will be modest. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who refused the deal, described it as “peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta’s profit-driven addictive features inflicted on kids.” Meta’s stock shot up 4 percent on news of the settlement, which, at the high mark, added roughly $59 billion to the company’s market value — well above the entire settlement, in one day.

It smacks of another Cambridge Analytica settlement . In 2018, it was reported that Meta (then called Facebook) might owe the Federal Trade Commission $2 trillion . But the fine levied was only $5 billion, and its stock rose immediately upon the announcement.

When a company’s stock goes up the day a penalty is announced, something is amiss.

The implications of this case go beyond Meta. California Attorney General Rob Bonta stated that Meta is simply “ first in line .” YouTube, TikTok and Snap all face similar cases. $5 billion of Meta’s payout only gets paid if YouTube and TikTok adopt the same changes. In essence, Meta has turned the attorneys general into enforcers against its competitors , ensuring kids won’t switch to other apps.

Outside the courtroom, the response has been stronger. Nearly 30 states launched bell-to-bell phone bans in schools in recent years. A Senate committee advanced the Kids Online Safety Act this August. Last year, Australia became the first country to bar users under 16 from social media, with other countries following suit. The European Union is also moving toward a ban of its own .

Thousands of individual and school district lawsuits remain on the docket. Meta admitted no wrongdoing , but there’s plenty of ground remaining to be taken in these upcoming cases.

The attorneys general wanted a result, and they got one. But Meta walked away with a bargain. Were the states outmaneuvered? The plaintiffs who took Meta to court this year in Los Angeles and New Mexico won their cases. The thousands of families and school districts still waiting have strong cases too.

The lesson: Don’t settle. Make Meta face a jury.

articles.title: In Florida, illegal aliens who commit crimes aren’t deported — they’re put to death
articles.summary: The state of Florida has been dogged in its determination to become the death penalty capital of the nation. It allows non-unanimous juries to impose death sentences. It allows prosecutors to seek such sentences for people convicted of sexual battery against children under age 12. And in 2025, it passed a law making the death penalty mandatory for any illegal alien convicted of first-degree murder.…
articles.body:
The state of Florida has been dogged in its determination to become the death penalty capital of the nation. It allows non-unanimous juries to impose death sentences . It allows prosecutors to seek such sentences for people convicted of sexual battery against children under age 12. And in 2025, it passed a law making the death penalty mandatory for any illegal alien convicted of first-degree murder.

Last month, a prosecutor in Lake County became the first to use that law as the basis of a capital prosecution. State Attorney Bill Gladson is seeking the death penalty for Shahidul Islam, a Bangladeshi national. He is an illegal alien, who was deported but returned to the U.S. While here, he allegedly shot and killed his sister-in-law.

If Gladson succeeds in getting a death sentence, he will have pulled off a MAGA double-header, combining the movement’s embrace of capital punishment and its hostility toward people who enter the country illegally.

Recall that in October 2024, President Trump made that connection when he said, “I’m hereby calling for the death penalty for any migrant who kills an American citizen or a law enforcement officer.”

And on the first day of his second term, he issued an executive order directing the attorney general to “seek the death penalty regardless of other factors for every federal capital crime … committed by an alien illegally present in this country.” His order also encouraged states to adopt similar policies.

That is why you can be sure that Trump administration officials will be following Islam’s prosecution closely.

It is no coincidence that the law under which he is being charged is called the TRUMP Act , and that it cites several of the president’s anti-immigration initiatives in the law itself. In the words of the law , “the Legislature finds it necessary to rigorously implement both the letter and spirit of Trump’s plan to secure our border, protect our state and national sovereignty, support Florida law enforcement, and affirm the federal government’s responsibility over immigration.”

In addition, if Gladson succeeds in securing a mandatory death sentence for Shahidul Islam, it will tee up a challenge for the Supreme Court. Fifty years ago, the court held that the death penalty could never be made mandatory or imposed automatically .

The law’s supporters knew what they were doing. As one of them put it , “We have cho­sen to pass things that we knew were uncon­sti­tu­tion­al at the time we passed them, because we believed the Supreme Court would change their minds.” That is not how the Supreme Court has ever understood what the Constitution requires in capital cases. If the Islam case ever reaches the court, it should not change its stance.

In 1976, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a statute that made the death penalty mandatory for specified crimes. Writing for the majority, Justice Potter Stewart explained : “In capital cases the fundamental respect for humanity underlying the Eighth Amendment requires consideration of the character and record of the individual offender and the circumstances of the particular offense as a constitutionally indispensable part of the process of inflicting the penalty of death.”

He added that manda­to­ry death sentences treat defendants as “a faceless, undifferentiated mass.”

That is exactly what Gladson is trying to do with Islam. He made that clear during a press conference announcing the prosecution, calling the crime “ completely preventable ” and laying the blame on the Biden administration’s open border policy.

Gladson praised the state’s illegal alien law and its mandatory death penalty provision. He said that it gives notice to people who are in this country illegally that if they commit a capital crime, they will not be deported. Instead, he said, “they will face the trial of their life.”

The state attorney and his colleagues made clear that they care little about why Islam may have committed the crime with which he is charged, or about the circumstances that may have contributed to it. For them, he is a stand-in for, and symbol of, a nation allegedly overrun by illegal immigrants.

It seems not to matter to them that, in fact, illegal immigrants are less likely to commit violent crimes and homicides than people born in the U.S. And it is ironic that in a state so devoted to enforcing the law, Islam is being prosecuted under a law that is itself of questionable legality.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.
