articles.title: House returns after five weeks away with a top priority: Avoid a government shutdown
articles.summary: The House is back ith a top priority of avoiding a government shutdown before the midterm elections.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The House is scheduled to return Monday from a five-week summer recess with a top priority of avoiding a government shutdown before the midterm elections. The House will only be in session for four days this week and will return again Sept. 14, after Labor Day, when the Senate will also come back from its lengthy break. From there, the House has just three weeks left in session before Election Day on Nov. 3. Here’s what could be on the agenda for House Republican leaders before the midterms, when their paper-thin majority will be on the line: Fund the government and prevent a shutdown This week, the House is expected to take up a Senate-passed bill to prevent a government shutdown, according to a Republican leadership aide. Money is currently expected to expire for federal departments and agencies Oct. 1. It’s the main item on the agenda, the only critical deadline requiring action before the midterm elections. If it passes, the bill would go to President Donald Trump to become law and keep funds flowing through Dec. 11. That would buy time for a larger government funding deal, on which negotiations have stalled. The result of the midterm elections will shape the talks, with the 2026 winners likely to feel empowered. The legislation passed the Senate by a vote of 90-6, continuing funding on autopilot without major changes and thereby staying noncontroversial. It includes a few add-ons that were negotiated by both parties: restricting Trump’s power to cut off federal grants to blue states that didn’t vote for him and preserving food assistance programs such as SNAP and WIC, as well as disaster relief. The bill is expected to be fast-tracked to the House floor on “suspension,” skipping committee hurdles and requiring a two-thirds majority to pass. It’s likely to pass by a big margin, unless Trump jumps in with last-minute demands as he has with some past funding deals. Chuck Edwards censure vote During the August recess, the bipartisan House Ethics Committee said that it was recommending that the full chamber vote to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., after its monthslong investigation found that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” The House could take that vote as soon as this week. If a censure resolution does come to the floor, it is expected to pass given that only a handful of Republicans would need to team with all 212 Democrats for a successful vote. Shortly after the censure recommendation, Edwards said he was dropping his bid for re-election and would not appear on the ballot in November. But Edwards, who has disputed the Ethics panel’s findings, is aggressively fighting to defeat the censure vote. Last week, he reportedly sent a 22-page letter to colleagues defending his actions and arguing that nothing found by the probe could be construed as “sexual misconduct.” “An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition,” he wrote. Censure is a formal rebuke of a member of Congress; after a successful vote, the member is typically required to stand in the well of the House chamber while the resolution is read aloud. But censure does not remove the lawmaker from office. Also on the ethics front, the House will vote on two contempt of Congress resolutions recommended by the Ethics Committee related to the panel’s investigation of former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, D-Fla. The committee recommended finding both Michael Joseph, mayor of North Miami Beach, and Hector Roos, a Florida political operative, in contempt for refusing to comply with subpoenas in that probe. Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April after the Ethics Committee found her guilty of 25 ethics violations and as it prepared to consider expelling her from Congress. Iran and Russia sanctions One potential item on the upcoming House agenda is a bill passed by the Senate to slap new sanctions on Russia and Iran. The House has no plans to vote on it this week, but it remains a possibility in the foreseeable future. The legislation, approved by the Senate on a vote of 86-11 in early August, is called the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named after the late senator whose sudden death in July fueled support for the cause he had long supported. The bill aims to punish the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas and paves the way for sanctions against Russian leaders, family members and oligarchs. It also allows the U.S. to impose targeted tariffs on goods from countries that buy most Russian oil and gas, more specifically the five biggest importers.

articles.body:
President Trump vowed to respond to Iran’s retaliatory strikes on Monday after the two countries exchanged strikes late Sunday.

“We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response,” Trump told Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst.

The president’s remarks to Fox News come after he lashed out at Iran in a TruthSocial post, calling it a “failed nation.”

“They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country,” Trump wrote on Monday. “The only thing they have is FAKE NEWS from the USA, a willingness to kill their protesters (now over 100,000 people dead. They must be tried for war crimes against humanity!), and a good line of ‘BULL—-.’”

The U.S. launched its first attack on Iran in over a month on Sunday, striking two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island.

A Central Command spokesman said the attack came after U.S. forces said they observed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran retaliated early on Monday, targeting U.S. military assets at bases in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Jordan.

“Aggression and crimes will not solve the enemy’s desperation in attempting to weaken the Islamic Republic’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and every attack will be met with even more devastating responses,” the IRGC said in a statement to the Iranian state-run Fars News Agency.

The exchange in strikes between the countries led to a spike in oil prices on Monday.

September futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 3.4 percent to trade at $91.09 per barrel early Monday morning, after seeing a sharp fall last week. West Texas Intermediate futures also rose 3.4 percent, with trading at $86.22 per barrel.

articles.title: Trump knocks ‘highly conflicted’ judge in Kennedy Center case
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday knocked U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who has overseen the case over the Kennedy Center and the president’s attempts to refurbish and rename the living memorial, as “highly conflicted.” “Kennedy Center is an old and decrepit building that is badly in need of a major construction and public relations fix before…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday knocked U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who has overseen the case over the Kennedy Center and the president’s attempts to refurbish and rename the living memorial, as “highly conflicted.”

“Kennedy Center is an old and decrepit building that is badly in need of a major construction and public relations fix before it can attain greatness and prestige, perhaps far greater than ever before,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“It has been losing a fortune for many years, and will continue to do so if the highly conflicted judge on the case doesn’t allow us to do what has to be done!” he added.

Cooper, appointed by former President Obama, ruled that Trump’s name cannot be added to the building, having ordered the lettering outside the building to be removed . He said that only Congress can change the center’s name, as the building was established by Congress as a living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy.

The signage outside the building was covered with a tarp .

Trump’s description of the building mirrors those said by Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers, who said in court filings last Monday that the Kennedy Center was a “decrepit” structure in severe need of renovations or demolition .

The administration has said the building is in need of extensive repairs. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday that the planned renovation is expected to cost $257 million.

Lutnick also floated the idea of adding Trump’s name to the building by means of an acknowledgment stating that the president renovated the building.

“Underneath the name of the building, which will remain the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump,” he said.

The Kennedy Center board, having agreed to hold off on renewing Trump’s name to the performing arts center, voted to add an inscription underneath the Kennedy Center’s name that reads: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the center’s board who has successfully challenged Trump’s proposed changes to building in court, said Saturday that the legal battle could prevent Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center.

“This started back in December of 2025, so I’m a little more hopeful with this because we are in court,” Beatty said on MS NOW. “He may have thought about doing it when he was ordered to take his name down. So I think there is a slight difference.

articles.title: Can Iowa Democrats help the national party appeal to working-class voters?
articles.summary: Democratic candidates Josh Turek and Rob Sand are attempting to reach working-class white male voters in Iowa by focusing on issues like healthcare, government efficiency, and right-to-repair legislation.
articles.body:
That line was spoken in one of my favorite movies of all time — 1989’s “Field of Dreams.”

As a journalist covering Iowa’s presidential caucuses I once drove through farmland to achieve a dream of my own — I wanted to stand on baseball’s legendary “Field of Dreams .”

Today, Democrats have another kind of dream coming to life in Iowa. They can see effective political appeals by Democrats to working-class, white men. These are voters who in the last decade turned away from Democrats and became star players in the political base that launched national victories for President Trump.

Now Iowa is offering a preview of a possibly big change. In the Iowa races for the U.S. Senate and for governor, Democrats have nominated candidates gaining traction with working class white men: Josh Turek, the candidate for U.S. Senate and state Auditor Rob Sand, the party’s gubernatorial nominee.

Turek has produced the best political advertisement of this midterm political cycle. The spot features Turek playing a driveway basketball game, a game of “HORSE,” changing the letters to “IOWA.” His opponent is the last Democratic presidential nominee to win Iowa, President Barack Obama.

“I know a little something about winning Iowa,” Obama says, a reference to his 2008 caucus victory that propelled the little-known U.S. senator from Illinois to the Democratic presidential nomination . Obama also carried Iowa in both the 2008 and 2012 general elections.

“Of all the things I’ve done in politics, Iowa was my favorite thing,” Obama tells Turek in the ad . “There was just a magic about regular folks showing up.”

It is an eye-grabbing advertisement. Turek, the winner of two gold medals in wheelchair basketball as a Paralympian , shows his basketball shooting skill in defeating Obama.

The ad shows his skill as a competitor and one of the guys in a gym as he runs against right-wing Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson.

Beyond the ad, Turek is effectively pressing Hinson on her votes for Trump’s Medicare cuts which devastated rural health care in the Hawkeye State.

The nonpartisan Kaiser Family Foundation estimates the Trump cuts will limit healthcare for as many as 100,000 Iowans. Eight rural hospitals are at risk of closure.

In the governor’s race, Sand is running on his record since 2019 as the state’s auditor.

He is presenting himself as more intent on delivering waste-free government than the GOP officials now dominating the state’s politics.

At campaign rallies, Sand, the lone Democrat in statewide office in Iowa, makes a point of starting off with a chorus of “God Bless America ” — a powerful symbol to separate himself from Trump’s constant attacks on Democrats as lacking patriotism because they disagree with his war in Iran.

Sand is also getting an assist from the drip, drip, drip of negative stories about his Republican opponent, who appears to live in Kansas and was a major investor in a company that made award-winning sex toys .

Iowa has not had a Democratic governor in 15 years. Turek’s campaign for the U.S. Senate is also facing a Democratic drought. Iowa has not had a Democrat in the U.S. Senate in more than a decade, and it hasn’t elected a Democrat in nearly two decades.

That senator, Tom Harkin, served for 30 years. Now 86, Harkin has endorsed Turek .

Both of the insurgent Democrats must fight the polarized media of the Trump era, which puts blinders on voters trying to look across party lines.

In the cookie-cutter stereotypes offered nationwide, the Democratic Party is often labeled as the party of “weak and woke,” to quote Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). Paul Begala, the former Clinton White House aide, once remarked that the Democratic Party began to lose ground when it became “the party of the faculty lounge instead of the factory floor.”

Turek and Sand also have to confront conservative media portrayals of Democrats as uniformly supporting the far left of the party, the democratic socialists. The challenge in Iowa and other states is to defy these caricatures.

Iowa is fertile ground for Democrats on that front because engaged voters can expect to see candidates in person, if not talk with them.

For that reason, the Iowa State Fair, one of the most popular in the nation, is regularly attended by candidates of both parties, including presidential aspirants. Sen. Mark Kelly (D- Ariz.) was there last week .

Paid advertising is also less expensive in Iowa than massive media markets in states like Florida and Texas. Again, Iowa gives Democrats a better chance to remind rural and small-town voters, including a large share of Christian Evangelicals, about the negatives of the Trump record.

Specifically, Trump’s tariffs, most recently imposed against nearby Canada, could hurt Iowa farmers .

For decades, Republican lawmakers have allowed large equipment manufacturers like John Deere to monopolize the market on repairing farm equipment, only very recently allowing the people using the equipment to make some routine repairs on their own.

Democrats like Sand and Turek are reminding farmers they support “right to repair” legislation that would save them time and money.

Turek and Sand are creating political messages with potential to become the prescriptive model for effective Democratic appeals to the voters who previously lined up with Trump.

It is a pattern with potential to go nationwide: If you build it, they will come.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Paxton responds to Cornyn calling him ‘lazy’: ‘They don’t know my schedule’
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) on Sunday pushed back on Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) calling him a “lazy” campaigner. “John Cornyn doesn’t know my schedule. He doesn’t know how many hours I’m putting in every day, 18 hours a day,” Paxton told host Jacqui Heinrich on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing.” Paxton, who beat…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) on Sunday pushed back on Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) calling him a “lazy” campaigner.

“John Cornyn doesn’t know my schedule. He doesn’t know how many hours I’m putting in every day, 18 hours a day,” Paxton told host Jacqui Heinrich on Fox News’s “ The Sunday Briefing .”

Paxton, who beat Cornyn by more than 27 points in May’s Texas Senate GOP runoff, added he has been “driving all over the state,” raising money and trying his “best to connect to as many voters as possible.”

The Republican nominee continued, “They don’t know my schedule. It’s completely fabricated.”

Earlier this month, Cornyn told The Texas Tribune that while he supports the party’s ticket in Texas, his former primary opponent is at risk of losing to Democratic nominee James Talarico in November.

“Paxton’s a poor campaigner,” Cornyn said. “He’s lazy and doesn’t raise money. And he basically is not offering a very compelling case for his election. He’s making this harder than it needs to be. But so be it — we are where we are.”

But Paxton said Sunday he is averaging roughly 18 hours of campaigning per day in the general election sprint and stopped in “four or five different cities” on Saturday alone.

Polling indicates a tight race between Paxton and Talarico, a member of the Texas House since 2018.

A recent survey from Texas Public Opinion Research found Talarico leading with 47 percent support to Paxton’s 40 percent, with 11 percent of respondents undecided. Talarico’s lead was outside the margin of error of 3.3 percentage points.

Decision Desk HQ also gave Talarico a 55 percent chance to win as of Thursday, as the 37-year-old attempts to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State since former Sen. Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

One edge Talarico has over Paxton is his campaign war chest. As of the end of June, the Democrat’s campaign had more than $21.5 million on hand compared with less than $1.8 million for the Republican’s operation, according to the Federal Election Commission.

But Paxton set up a joint fundraising committee with the National Republican Senatorial Committee in June, after the group bashed him during the primary.

The state attorney general also said Sunday he has reached out to “many” Cornyn donors, an endeavor he started “immediately” after the runoff.

“We are attracting Cornyn donors and Cornyn supporters, because I think they realize … if we lose this race, we’re going to lose the U.S. Senate and we’re going to lose Texas,” he told Heinrich.

“So we have to win this race, and we are going to win.”

articles.title: Trump: Reflecting Pool ‘almost completely fixed’ with improvements
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said the improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are “almost completely fixed.” Trump shared a photo of the grass near the World War II Memorial on the National Mall, where an etching of “86 47” was seen in the grass in June. The aerial shot also showed the Lincoln Memorial…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said the improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are “almost completely fixed.”

Trump shared a photo of the grass near the World War II Memorial on the National Mall, where an etching of “86 47” was seen in the grass in June. The aerial shot also showed the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which underwent renovations that were met with public scrutiny.

“Look what VANDALS did to the grass connecting the vandalized World War II Monument and the vandalized Reflecting Pool, which will be opened again, and better than ever, shortly,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn’t vandalized should go back to Law School!” he continued. “The grass is being replaced shortly, and the Reflecting Pool is almost completely fixed, including the various inflow and outflow pipes, which we were saving for the end of the year, but will do now.”

Trump on Friday quoted the Interior Department in saying the latest Reflecting Pool renovations were “ coming out great! ” His Truth Social post noted the pool was partially refilled to allow National Park Service staff and contractors to flush the piping system.

The state of the Reflecting Pool has been a source of controversy for months. Trump repeatedly touted the multimillion-dollar project while it was underway, but it appeared to be gray and peeling after it was completed.

Trump has insisted the pieces of “American flag blue” coating and algae blooms seen in the Reflecting Pool were perpetrated by vandals .

The Department of Justice (DOJ) charged several people, including Olympic canoeist David Hearn, in connection with the damage to the pool, accusing Hearn of damaging the pool with his bare hands. The charges were later dropped , with U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro saying the issues with the pool were caused by botched renovations.

Trump later accused Pirro of having “choked” in her decision to drop the charges.

Trump, too, said there was “ some contractor error ” with the renovations. Last week, he quoted the Interior Department in requesting “ NO VANDALS PLEASE .”

The “86 47” in the grass, seen days before the UFC Freedom 250 match outside the White House on Trump’s birthday, has become a reference to showing opposition to Trump, with “86” commonly used in the food and beverage industry to refer to items or ingredients no longer available or removed.

The president has claimed the numbers are a threat to him, most notably after former FBI Director James Comey shared a photo of seashells shaped to spell out the numbers on social media last year. The post led the DOJ to indict Comey , who moved to dismiss the case last month.

articles.title: Met Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano canceled
articles.summary: The Met’s Galliano retrospective exhibition announcement received widespread backlash due to his past antisemitic and racist statements.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The Metropolitan Museum of Art canceled its spring 2027 exhibit honoring designer John Galliano Monday, casting uncertainty over next year’s Met Gala, which annually serves as the opening event.

“Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition,” museum director Max Hollein said in a statement.

The Met’s July announcement to honor Galliano received widespread backlash due to antisemitic and racist statements the designer made in 2010 and 2011.

In a social media post, Galliano apologized for the remarks and withdrew from the exhibition.

“After much reflection and discussion with The Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” he wrote. “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.”

Despite being convicted in a French court for his words in 2011, Galliano remains a widely celebrated fixture of the fashion world for his designs . He reached widespread fame as creative director of Christian Dior, which dropped him after 15 years when the remarks surfaced. He then led the fashion house Maison Margiela in 2014, where he remained for a decade. He’s a favorite designer and longtime friend of Anna Wintour, who organizes the Met Gala each year.

The museum says the exhibit will be replaced by another show.

articles.title: Iran war flares up on two fronts as Trump issues fresh threat
articles.summary: ⏰ House returns to face shutdown clock {beacon} It’s Monday … and the last day of August, as the end of summer rapidly approaches. Soak it up, 12:30 Report readers. In today’s issue: U.S., Iran resume strikes Pentagon on defense over leak House returns from monthlong break Bessent to invoke China at G20…
articles.body:
It’s Monday … and the last day of August, as the end of summer rapidly approaches. Soak it up, 12:30 Report readers.

Programming note: Hello! We are Elliott Davis , Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to edavis@thehill.com, cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com.

The Associated Press | Vahid Salemi and Mark Schiefelbein)

President Trump is promising to retaliate for Iran’s strikes on Jordan overnight Sunday, which came in response to the U.S. taking out two Iranian rocket launchers over the weekend.

“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Trey Yingst on Fox News. “There will be a response.”

The tit for tat ends a monthlong pause in fighting as Trump has shifted to a strategy of economic strangulation. Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, which was also targeted by Iranian strikes, said all incoming drones and missiles were shot down.

Markets don’t like it: Gas prices ticked up and stocks dipped Monday morning in response to the exchange of fire — a reminder of the risks facing Trump if the fighting escalates further.

U.S. Central Command has pushed back on Iranian claims of “aggression,” accusing Iran’s Revolutionary Guard of “preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” from Larak Island into the Strait of Hormuz.

What negotiations? Qatar’s Foreign Ministry condemned Iran’s strikes on regional countries, warning the hostilities “complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions and undermine political and diplomatic efforts seeking to achieve security and stability in the region.”

Those efforts didn’t seem to be going so well even before the strikes.

Trump last week said the U.S. is in no rush to resume talks with Iran, pointing to steady oil flow out of the Strait of Hormuz and the mounting economic pressure on Tehran.

The Pentagon’s press shop went into overdrive this weekend in response to a Washington Post report about growing concerns among military leaders over continuing the Iran war.

Someone leaked the Aug. 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), in which Pete Hegseth reportedly directs some U.S. forces deployed in the Middle East to remain through September and others into 2027.

The heads of U.S. European, Pacific and Southern commands, along with the Navy’s top admiral, responded with a “non-concur” to that order — signaling their disagreement with prolonging the war.

The Pentagon was furious: “Publishing highly classified assessments from the Secretary’s orders book is a crime. It’s a betrayal of the force,” its top spokesperson, Sean Parnell , wrote on the social platform X. “And much of what they’re publishing is inaccurate.”

The pushback also came from some notable X accounts with links to the Pentagon, including DataRepublican, whom The Hill’s Filip Timotija wrote about last week .

In a well-timed double whammy, the Post published this story on Sunday: Pentagon secretly installs military influencers in civilian roles

Lawmakers will return to Capitol Hill later today for a short stint in session before another two-week recess.

There is much to accomplish over the next few days, including one large item: A Senate-passed stopgap measure, also known as a continuing resolution (CR), that would fund the government through Dec. 11.

The CR is expected to advance as it has support from Democrats and Republicans, The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi reports . If it does and Trump eventually signs it, Congress would avoid another government shutdown after last year’s record-breaker .

What else?: Other tasks on lawmakers’ list include a resolution condemning socialism in all its forms amid democratic socialist candidates’ recent success in primaries, the Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill and a potential resolution to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) over sexual harassment allegations .

Wait … another recess is coming?: Yes. The House is set to be in session four days this week and then will return — alongside the Senate — on Sept. 14, after the Labor Day holiday.

➤ MARKEY, MOULTON SET FOR PRIMARY BATTLE:

Two Massachusetts Democrats, Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton , will face off tomorrow in the Bay State’s Senate primary that has become a generational battle of sorts.

Moulton, 47, has argued that a “new generation of leaders” is needed, mocking Markey, 80, at a recent debate over the incumbent saying he uses “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad” in response to a question about the use of AI platforms at work.

But in an Emerson College Polling survey released Sunday, Markey had a comfortable lead of 60.4 percent to 32.8 percent over his challenger.

Elsewhere in Massachusetts, six candidates are vying for the Democratic nomination in the 6th Congressional District on Tuesday, while Rep. Stephen Lynch (D) is facing a progressive challenger in the 8th Congressional District.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is bringing the China trade fight to the G20 — and he’s calling for backup.

Bessent plans to urge fellow finance ministers to take a harder look at their economic relationships with Beijing, arguing China’s roughly $1.2 trillion trade surplus is a problem that can’t be left for the U.S. to tackle alone.

The Treasury chief will host G20 finance ministers Monday and Tuesday in Asheville, N.C., before the U.S. hosts the leaders’ summit in Miami in December.

Little room for dealmaking : Bessent said the U.S. and China could each remove tariffs on about $30 billion worth of nonstrategic goods when Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet in Washington next month.

Bottom line: He wants other countries to take a closer look at what they’re buying from China — and how much they’re willing to keep absorbing.

China is Iran’s biggest trading partner and primary buyer of its oil, putting Beijing in the crosshairs of Trump’s pressure campaign on the Islamic Republic.

Bessent has urged Beijing to get with the program, but the Chinese government has pushed back , saying potential U.S. sanctions will only raise tensions.

Trump also weighed in Monday on growing backlash to data centers, arguing communities have more to gain than lose by welcoming the centers.

In a Truth Social post , the president said data centers can bring jobs, economic growth and lower taxes — and warned that turning them away could push those benefits to communities elsewhere.

He also pointed to China, saying Beijing “could not be happier” to see opposition to the centers growing amid the AI arms race .

📺 Trump is threatening to report NBC host Kristen Welker to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) after she said his endorsed candidates have had “mixed results” during the primaries. At least one FCC commissioner has pushed back on the move.

👨‍⚖️ The president ripped the judge overseeing his Kennedy Center case as “highly conflicted” as he pushes to renovate and put his name back on the building. He also doubled down on his plans for the center, calling the building “old and decrepit” and badly in need of a major overhaul.

🏀 Billionaire Mark Walter ’s abrupt sale of the Los Angeles Lakers is raising fresh questions about ownership in pro sports and shining a spotlight on how teams are increasingly being treated like financial assets. Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo .

⚖️ Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) is floating a major shake-up of the Supreme Court. He says a “baker’s dozen” — or 13 justices — would be a “pretty good number” for the high court.

Politico: The Trump-shaped problems awaiting Andy Burnham, ranked

The New York Times: Millions of Dollars in Secret Spending Could Upend the 2026 Midterms

Wall Street Journal: Russia Turns to New-Generation Drones and All-Day Attacks to Wear Down Ukrainians

The Los Angeles Times: AI is watching your spending and setting your prices accordingly. Lawmakers want to stop it

articles.body:
Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) on Sunday said former President Biden and his administration should have released the federal government’s documents and files connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Frost appeared on Jubilee’s “Surrounded,” where a guest confronted him about President Trump before the lawmaker asked if he did not believe the president has been “covering up the Epstein files,” accusing Trump of such an attempt. The guest pushed back and asked why the Biden administration did not release the files.

“They should have,” Frost replied. “They should have.”

“No, they should have, but they didn’t. You know why they didn’t? Because he’s the most corrupt president ever,” the guest yelled back in reference to Biden, with other guests applauding.

Frost repeated that the Biden administration should have released it before adding that Trump campaigned on releasing the files.

“He said, ‘Release the files,'” the Florida Democrat continued. “He literally said he would release the files. He said at multiple campaign rallies that he was going to release the files. … So, we’re holding him accountable to that.

Frost also mentioned that the files were released after Reps. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) authored a bill that passed Congress after compelling House members to a floor vote in November, with the assistance of Reps. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.).

The legislation, which Trump signed into law, required the Department of Justice (DOJ) to release all of its documents, with redactions in place to protect the identities of survivors and any individuals possibly under investigation.

But the DOJ’s rollout of the files, along with heavy redactions and missing redactions, was met with heavy scrutiny from the public and lawmakers.

In December, former Vice President Kamala Harris defended the Biden administration for not requesting the DOJ to release the files. She told late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that the administration “strongly and rightly believed that there should be an absolute separation between what we wanted as an administration and what the Department of Justice did.”

Trump asked in July 2025 why Democrats did not go ahead and release the files while they controlled the White House and Senate. He accused Democrats of perpetuating a “SCAM,” claiming that Biden’s DOJ “HAD NOTHING!”

The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, in its ongoing probe into Epstein, his crimes and his associates, has received testimony from several people, including former President Clinton, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, lawyer Alan Dershowitz and former Attorney General Pam Bondi, who was criticized for how the release of the DOJ’s documents on Epstein was handled.

The committee, including nine Democrats , voted to hold the Clintons in contempt. Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) sought to penalize the political couple for failing to respond to a congressional subpoena tied to the probe. Both later testified.

Comer has also formally requested Dershowitz to testify. Dershowitz told NewsNation in June that he was willing to sit for a videotaped interview with the committee.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed still fails to denounce Hasan Piker
articles.summary: Now that El-Sayed is competing in a general election for the votes of normies, including many Jewish Michiganders who don’t at all appreciate what Piker has said about Israel, El-Sayed is not sure what to do.
articles.body:
Apparently, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed just can’t bring himself to condemn and distance himself from controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

Recall that El-Sayed happily palled around with Piker, who said America deserved 9/11 and that authoritarian China is the ideal form of government , when he wanted to cash in on his cred to win the Democratic primary. But now that El-Sayed is competing in a general election for the votes of normies, including many Jewish Michiganders who don’t at all appreciate what Piker has said about Israel, El-Sayed is not sure what to do.

When he wanted Piker’s help, he was happy to bring him to Michigan, but now that Piker is a liability, he’s just some guy from California. How convenient!

On CNN, Democratic strategist Faiz Shakir tried — and, may I say, failed — to explain why El-Sayed shouldn’t have to say anything about Piker.

First of all, I don’t want ever again want to hear about Donald Trump dining with Nick Fuentes as some gotcha comment. Trump dined with Kanye West, who brought Fuentes to the dinner. Trump didn’t know who Fuentes was. If El-Sayed had gone out to dinner and been randomly seated at the same table as Piker, we would not be making a big deal about this. But that’s not what happened. El-Sayed chose Piker. Trump did not choose Fuentes. This is not an equivalent transgression.

Moreover, Trump is not on the ballot in Michigan! This isn’t really about Trump. It’s about what is right for the residents of that state: a senator who is frankly a fairly standard Republican, and a senator who represents the far-left fringe of the Democratic Party.

Also, it’s a bit rich for Democrats and liberal media figures to be complaining about cancel culture now. They’re just whining because they are largely out of power. If they had the same ability to summon social media mobs to denounce problematic persons and have their associates punished, the way they did eight years ago, of course they would be out for blood. I appreciate that Shakir never thought it made sense to cancel Joe Rogan, though that’s because at the time Rogan was actually a supporter of Shakir’s boss, Bernie Sanders. But so many Democrats made every effort to condemn people who made allegedly offensive statements. Tony Hinchcliffe ? Hinchcliffe is a comedian. And the right did condemn him! Again, there is no equivalency!

I think most of the people who are so mad that this controversy has legs are actually mad not because the standard is unfair, but rather secretly it’s because they don’t have a big problem with the things Piker says. Maybe they wish he wouldn’t say them, because his words are getting Democrats in so much trouble! But they kinda see his point about America deserving 9/11.

That’s because, in the left’s imagining of things, America is always the bad guy. Now most Americans, obviously, do not agree with that. The question becomes, are we ready to elect to Congress people who feel that way? People who represent the leftist fringe? Time will tell.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: ‘Rebuke or punishment’: Trump threatens to report Kristen Welker to FCC
articles.summary: Press can be criticized, but the president cannot use the power of the federal government as a threat against a journalist because the coverage is unfavorable.
articles.body:
President Trump lashed out at “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker on Sunday, suggesting she would be reported to the Federal Communications Commission over her alleged characterization of primary election results.

Apparently, during a pre-show live shot with a local DC station, Welker reportedly said the president had “mixed results” with candidates he has endorsed during this cycle.

Welker didn’t say Trump’s endorsements were failing. She acknowledged his influence while also noting that he had suffered some losses.

On Truth Social, he called Welker the “Unpopular ‘Hostess’” of “Meet the Fake Press” and accused her of “purposeful inaccuracy.” He then wrote, “she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

The president went on to describe the press in his truth social post as a “Disgrace to our Nation,” and directly suggested FCC Chair Brendan Carr take this “threat to our country very seriously.”

While Trump’s overall primary win rate remains high, he has faced some notable setbacks, particularly in high-profile gubernatorial races and house races this year, like former MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell’s primary loss for governor of Minnesota and Republican Florida voters rebuking embattled congressman Cory Mills .

The FCC is a federal regulator. It is not supposed to be the president’s personal referee for whether a journalist’s characterization of his political record is flattering enough.

The commission under Brenden Carr’s leadership has already faced bipartisan criticism. Late last year, several former FCC officials filed a petition asking the commission to remove its “news distortion policy,” which it notes Carr has cited in threatening to crack down on mainstream media coverage that is critical of Trump.

So when Trump publicly calls on the FCC Chair to take yet another one of his complaints about the press “very seriously,” it feels less about accuracy and more about control.

Carr started in this role back January of 2025 ordering an investigation of NPR and PBS , after the president made it clear he had his eye on unraveling federal funding for all public broadcasting. He has launched investigations into ABC and targeted the network after the president made his disdain for the network apparent. In March of this year, he threatened the licenses of local broadcasters regarding their coverage of foreign conflicts like the Iran war, following complaints raised by the president on social media.

You may remember earlier this year, the president sat down with Kristen Welker and insisted the 2020 election was rigged :

TRUMP: “The election was rigged, it was a dirty election. And it’s happening again right now in California.”

WELKER: “You’ve never presented evidence that the 2020 election was rigged. Where’s the evidence to that? Republicans are doing well in California”

TRUMP: No, they’re not, they’re dropping fast because it’s a rigged election. It takes four days, they’re cheating.”

WELKER: “Do you have evidence to support that?”

The exchange resulted in the president abruptly leaving the interview :

TRUMP: “YOUR ELECTIONS ARE CROOKED AND YOU’RE CROOKED AND SO IS NBC, AND CNN. I’m done”

WELKER : “Mr. President, please, I’ve traveled all the way to Wisconsin.”

So this latest push by the president to have NBC and Welker reported feels connected to their interview.

Press can be criticized, but the president cannot use the power of the federal government as a threat against a journalist because the coverage is unfavorable.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.body:
Vice President Vance told reporters on Monday that President Trump was sending a message to Iran by posting what appears to be an AI-generated video of Iran’s Kharg Island being blown up.

Trump “would be the first to say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s sending a message to the Iranians,” Vance said at Joint Base Andrews en route to a stop in Michigan.

“Look, we know that they continue to shoot at commercial shipping. We continue to have a lot of tools at our disposal to prevent them from doing so, or at least cut down on them from doing so,” he continued. “And that’s what the president is saying is, ‘Look, you guys are shooting at commercial shipping. You guys are behaving like a terrorist country. You’ve got to stop, or there’s going to be some consequences.'”

The U.S. and Iran exchanged strikes on Sunday after the U.S. struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island. The strike marked the first between the two countries in more than a month.

A U.S. Central Command spokesperson noted the attack came after U.S. forces said they observed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran retaliated early Monday, targeting U.S. military assets at bases in the United Arab Emirates and Jordan.

“Aggression and crimes will not solve the enemy’s desperation in attempting to weaken the Islamic Republic’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and every attack will be met with even more devastating responses,” the IRGC said in a statement to the Iranian state-run Fars News Agency.

Trump vowed to respond to Iran’s retaliatory strikes during an interview with Fox News on Monday.

“We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response,” Trump said.

articles.title: Republicans will pay for Trump’s tariffs in the midterms
articles.summary: Ultimately, the 2026 midterms were always going to be an uphill battle for Republicans.
articles.body:
With midterms rapidly approaching, Republicans had appeared to catch a break on the economy.

After a year in which the war with Iran sent gas prices soaring and pushed inflation to multi-year highs, both June and July’s Consumer Price Index came in tame. Even grocery prices slipped for the first time in months.

But then President Trump returned to his longtime obsession: tariffs.

Indeed, last weekend, talks between the White House and Canada collapsed, and Trump immediately slapped 50 percent tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of Canadian goods, reviving what the Wall Street Journal called “The Dumbest Trade War in History.”

The timing could hardly be worse for Republicans, who had spent months straining to soothe voters’ concerns over the cost of living and attempting to build a midterm message around affordability. Now, tariffs and trade chaos are back in the news, and Republicans are likely going to pay the price.

As the Wall Street Journal noted , “Republicans are already getting pounded on the campaign trail over [Trump’s] tariffs and inflation.” The data confirm that. A majority of Americans, 56 percent, ranked cost of living concerns among the top issues facing the country, according to polling by Politico . Even among Trump voters, a plurality of 33 percent cite rising prices as “among the biggest failures of Trump’s second term.”

To be sure, voters have long disliked tariffs. March’s Harris Poll revealed that 72 percent of Americans — including 60 percent of Republicans — believe Trump’s tariffs have a negative impact.

Opinions have not changed, and evidence of the political implications is emerging. A 54 percent majority of likely voters in battleground states disapprove of the tariffs, according to New York Times-Siena polling , which surveyed voters in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.

The result? Reuters-Ipsos polling showed that voters now prefer Democrats’ approach to affordability over the Republicans’ approach by an 8-point margin (36 percent to 28 percent). Moreover, Democrats’ lead in the generic congressional ballot now sits slightly above 6 points, the widest margin of the cycle.

Trump’s overall approval rating is hovering just under 40 percent — more than 17 points underwater. Even key GOP constituencies like ranchers are angry at Trump’s efforts to improve affordability elsewhere by removing tariffs on imported beef.

On the economy, once Trump’s signature strength, his approval has sunk to 34.5 percent and more than 62 percent disapprove.

Republicans recognize the danger, but are powerless to stop it, even as it threatens to undermine what should have been a favorable Senate map. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) warned that the tariffs are causing “tension” and that “the party that owns that tension…will probably suffer the consequences in November.”

Compounding Republican concerns is that the states most affected by these new Canada tariffs are vital to Republicans’ hopes of holding onto the Senate. Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Alaska and Ohio are all extremely vulnerable to Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, and all have hotly contested races this fall.

Aware that tariffs are deeply unpopular and hoping to defend a key Senate seat, Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called the Canada tariffs a “mistake” before skipping an event with Vice President JD Vance in the state last week, where he defended the duties.

Former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.), who is trying to win back his old seat in New Hampshire, piled on, saying, “It makes no sense to start a trade war with our closest neighbor.”

Democrats are ready to take advantage, as the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spokesperson made clear , and the data suggests voters will be receptive to arguments that Trump and Republicans are “making life more expensive.”

While it is true that Trump is not entirely responsible for inflation, which has raged since the COVID-19 pandemic, that may matter little when voters are increasingly pessimistic about the economy, struggling to afford basic necessities, and looking for someone to blame.

Trump should know this well. In 2024, he benefitted from extreme discontent with “Bidenomics”. But now, Trump is actively keeping prices and tariffs in the headlines rather than telling voters how Republicans are working to lower costs.

At the same time, by waging trade wars, doubling down on tariffs, and dismissing affordability as “a fake word,” Trump lets Democrats off the hook for their own vulnerabilities, including an insurgent far left and a party favorability that is 14 points underwater.

Trump may not care about the midterms since he is not on the ballot, but he is seemingly intent on speeding up the date he will become a lame duck. And, in doing so, drastically increasing the chances of the “all-out oversight” investigations into himself and his family that Democrats are already preparing .

Ultimately, the 2026 midterms were always going to be an uphill battle for Republicans, as they always are for the party in power. In order to keep both the House and Senate — or at least one — the GOP needed a coherent affordability agenda and policies which lowered costs and strengthened the economy.

Instead, Republicans got renewed tariffs, for which they will likely pay the price in November.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. “

articles.title: Trump is using antisemitism claims as a pretext for a cash-grab
articles.summary: The contrived charges have obscured the very real incidents of antisemitism that have occurred on campuses and elsewhere.
articles.body:
The Trump administration corrupts almost everything it touches. Even seemingly commendable efforts to address very real social issues have turned out to be underhanded schemes to extract money from vulnerable institutions.

So it has been with the campaign against antisemitism on university campuses, as executed by a Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism under the Department of Justice and the Department of Health and Human Services. Largely focused on the pro-Palestine encampments set up in protest of Israel’s Gaza war, the administration’s accusations of pervasive antisemitism have been exposed as seriously exaggerated.

That is doubly unfortunate, because the contrived charges have obscured the very real incidents of antisemitism that have occurred on campuses and elsewhere.

In early 2025, Trump’s task force launched an investigation , under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, into alleged “antisemitic discrimination and harassment” at 60 colleges and universities, claiming that Jewish students “continue to fear for their safety amid the relentless antisemitic eruptions that have severely disrupted campus life.”

Prominent Ivy League universities were among the top targets, including Harvard, Columbia and Brown. Although based on actual incidents, the charges were overblown to say the least. They eventually fell apart almost completely, falling short of the prevalence and severity required by Title VI.

A former Justice Department attorney assigned to the task force recently submitted a whistleblower disclosure to Congress, asserting that the investigation had been a ruse to extort money from the universities.

According to the disclosure , the investigations had been “marked by extraordinary procedural irregularities, predetermined outcomes without factual or legal support, and disregard for Title VI’s legal requirements and the First Amendment,” all in a “politically mandated effort to disgorge enormous amounts of money from the universities.”

Despite the lack of evidence for pervasive discrimination, the Trump administration froze hundreds of millions in federal grants at targeted universities. Columbia and Brown eventually agreed to pay a total of $270 million to settle the administration’s claims of antisemitism and obtain the release of federal funding. Northwestern, where I am an emeritus professor, paid $75 million to settle antisemitism and other claims under similar terms.

Harvard refused to settle, leading to an enforcement action under Title VI, and a federal judge, dismissed the government’s case . Acknowledging the seriousness of cited antisemitic incidents, which included the storming of an event featuring an Israeli speaker, the court found them “singly and collectively, to be too isolated and episodic to support a plausible inference” of widespread discrimination.

Neither the court nor the whistleblower disclosure questioned the gravity of antisemitism on campuses. Rather, they concluded that the instances were not sufficiently extreme to meet the high threshold for enforcement actions under Title VI.

In a more honorable administration, the result of the investigations would most likely have been a descriptive report, outlining the actual occurrences of anti-Jewish rhetoric and conduct, while refraining from extortion in the guise of civil rights enforcement. Sadly but predictably, the administration’s overheated accusations have caused true antisemitic incidents at Gaza encampments to be discounted or denied.

What should have been an educational opportunity, addressing the moral distinction between political advocacy and threatening rhetoric, was lost once the Trump administration’s bullying entered the picture.

None of this absolves students who thoughtlessly joined antisemitic chants, such as “Globalize the Intifada,” which, although covered by the First Amendment, is no less offensive. Whatever the professed rationale of the protesters, the slogan is widely understood by Israelis and most Jews as an endorsement of indiscriminate violence against Jewish people and institutions around the world, irrespective of any connection to Israel or Zionism.

In Manchester , England, a driver globalized the Intifada by ramming his car into a synagogue on Yom Kippur, then stabbing two congregants to death. In Sydney , Australia, a father and son globalized the Intifada by massacring 15 people, and wounding dozens, on Bondi Beach at a “Hanukkah by the Sea” celebration. In Mumbai , gunmen from Lashkar-e-Taiba globalized the Intifada by invading a Jewish community center and murdering its rabbi and his wife.

Other such attacks are too numerous to list, occurring in Paris , Jersey City, Brussels , Monsey , New York, and Colleyville , Texas, among other locations.

Given that context, it ought to be possible to have a reasoned discussion of the chants and posters, explaining why “Globalizing the Intifada” has an effect on many Jews, regardless of intent — not unlike the Confederate Flag for African Americans. At least some Gaza protesters might choose a less threatening slogan.

Alas, we do not live in that world. Trump’s cynical use of antisemitism as a bludgeon against universities has, for many, made reasoned distinctions impossible. And everyone suffers.

Steven Lubet is the Williams Memorial Professor Emeritus at the Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law.

articles.title: Why we should care about what’s happening with Donald and Natalie
articles.summary: Trump’s obvious lack of concern for the well-being of most Americans helps explain why there’s such a fascination with the special treatment he affords Harp.
articles.body:
OK, let’s all take a deep breath and ask why we should care so much about the media melodrama swirling around President Donald Trump and one of his closest aides.

I mean, it’s shocking how much attention has been devoted to the entirely normal professional relationship between President Trump and his special assistant for obsessive flattery and late-night truth rants, Natalie Harp. Fortunately, noted feminists like Newt Gingrich have stepped up to defend the honor of “working professional women” everywhere from people who use “misogynistic language” to diminish and smear women who are “simply doing their job.”

Not that President Trump would ever use misogynistic language to smear, say, a journalist who is simply doing her job. Or a member of Congress. Or a Supreme Court justice.

You know, I don’t seem to remember many Republicans rallying to defend the working professional women, many of them women of color, who made up the majority of people purged in the mass firings of federal workers called for by Project 2025 and carried out by Elon Musk and Russell Vought. I don’t think the attitude expressed then was concern, as much as it was gloating.

We’re about to experience a similar disconnect between Republican posturing and Republican policies as Labor Day approaches.

While Trump campaigned as a champion of the “ forgotten men and women ,” he promptly forgot about them once he took power. While his henchmen ravaged worker protections , Trump focused on his real priorities: enriching himself and his family through brazen corruption .

In his first year since returning to power — even before his reckless decision to go to war against Iran had hiked gas prices and economic uncertainty —Trump had “actively made life less affordable for working people,” according to the Economic Policy Institute.

The biggest harm, the institute noted, was weakening workers’ bargaining power. “His policies have systematically stripped workers of leverage in the labor market, driving down pay and making it harder for working families to afford the basics,” it wrote. He’s the biggest union buster in American history.

In addition, the massive push for deregulation has made workers less safe and work riskier by robbing them of “of dozens upon dozens of rules that protect them from being forced to risk illness and injury on the job and ensure that they are paid for their labor.”

In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) released a report titled, “ 10 Ways President Trump Has Hurt American Workers .”

“Donald Trump promised American workers he’d have their backs, then turned on them once he took office,” said Sen. Warren. “He’s made it harder for workers to get a job and join a union, and easier for giant corporations to deny benefits and endanger workers.

In addition to rolling back health and safety regulations and undermining the National Labor Relations Board, Trump has harmed Americans by starting nonsensical trade wars with our closest allies and creating uncertainty with his erratic tariff policies.

The economic chaos and cultural fallout are hurting American workers and companies that make everything from bourbon to cars — and hurting communities and small businesses that rely on trade and tourism.

Meanwhile, Trump and his family have raked in billions of dollars . But it’s never enough. The new schemes keep coming . The latest is designed to make money for Trump and for Wall Street insiders who will pay big money for an early look at Trump social media posts designed to manipulate the stock market. One more way to rig the system against everyday people.

It’s clear that Trump doesn’t care about the people he’s hurting.

He doesn’t care about the soldiers and sailors who are bearing the brunt of the war he started without a plan to finish it. He’s told us he doesn’t worry about the war’s impact on workers and families who are struggling with the high cost of gas and the way that makes almost everything less affordable.

He doesn’t care about the immigrants and communities being terrorized by his mass deportation schemes. He doesn’t care about the kids and families being hurt by his administration’s undermining of public health measures like vaccines.

Trump’s obvious lack of concern for the well-being of most Americans helps explain why there’s such a fascination with the special treatment he affords Harp in return for her unsettling level of devotion. Even Cabinet members who regularly debase themselves to curry his favor were left on the plane that was deemed a security threat when Harp joined Trump in the infamous catering cart escape.

We know there are more important things happening in the world and our own lives. But we can’t help caring about this story, because it reveals so much about what Trump cares about. It isn’t us.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.body:
Vice President Vance lashed out at Democratic Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign style rally in Detroit on Monday, labeling him as “evil.”

“There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil, and on the rise in the United States of America today,” Vance said.

“It’s people who see themselves not as citizens of a combination, fighting for every single person, whether they’re Jewish or Christian, whether they’re white or black or brown, but see themselves as fighting for one group at the expense of others,” he continued. “And that is how, ladies and gentlemen, you destroy the United States of America.”

The vice president went on to knock El-Sayed for campaigning with far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker during the Democratic primary, and invoked Piker’s past comments saying the U.S. deserved the Sept. 11 terror attacks, which Piker has since apologized for.

“When I see Abdul El-Sayed campaign around this state with somebody who said that America deserved 9-11, what I see is a man who has sympathy and compassion for people who share his religion but have nothing for people who don’t,” Vance said. “A person who will apologize for a murderer so long as he looks the right way but will not understand the plight of an innocent child if that person has the wrong faith.”

Piker has taken a central role in the state’s Senate race despite not being on the ballot.

The streamer faced backlash on both sides of the aisle recently when he said “Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action.”

“Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” he said.

El-Sayed said in a statement responding to the backlash that “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”

He also noted that his commitment to Jewish safety “is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters,” referring to antisemitism as “a scourge.”

El-Sayed spent much of the weekend reaching out to the Jewish Democratic caucus in Michigan, and apologized for comments in March following an attack on a Detroit area synagogue in which he said “hurt people hurt people.”

“We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright. What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context, and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain,” El-Sayed told reporters over the weekend.

However, on Monday, Vance attacked El-Sayed over his response to the synagogue attack, and told his supporters that the synagogue’s rabbi and security guards were present at the event.

Ahead of Vance’s visit, El-Sayed swiped at what he called the chaotic nature of the Trump administration, while taking a shot at his general election opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.).

“Over the past couple of weeks, Michiganders have been struck by yet another disastrous Trump policy: the expansion of a trade war with Canada,” El-Sayed told reporters at a press conference. “With Mike Rogers, he has no choice but to rubber stamp, to ‘roger,’ a trade war that is now costing Michiganders—that he says he wants to serve—nearly $6,000 a year.”

“The choice could not be more clear. It is the chaos of the Trump administration, the cowardice of Mike Rogers, and the corruption of the entire MAGA party—or it’s a politics built on the notion that it should be people, rather than corporations and special interests, who dictate what our future looks like,” he said.
